utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we continue today I would like to ask you, Your Honours, if we could correct two or three errors that occurred in the transcript yesterday which I think are quite important for the understanding of the Defence case. At 12395, 20 to 21, it says that Witness Byrnes stated explicitly before this Trial Chamber that Sainovic had told him all he could in the negotiations, but what I actually did say Witness Byrnes stated explicitly before this Trial Chamber that Sainovic had told him that he had done all he could in the negotiating -- in the ongoing negotiations. So not "said" but "did." And at line 16, page 12046, when I talked about Exhibit P2862, it says -- the sentence begins with: "At this meeting," and what it actually should read is: "In this notebook ...," we're talking about General Vasiljevic's notebook. So this is all I had to say in this regard. Now, with your permission, I would like to continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we are grateful to you for reviewing the transcript in a matter as important as this, and that's a very helpful clarification you have given us. Please continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will continue now. This will be a little bit out of the context, but let me continue. What I said yesterday, that Sainovic had done all he could, we could illustrate this with an example when Judge Chowhan asked Witness Phillips regarding Sainovic's powers whether during the meetings, Sainovic had ever given any instructions or reprimanded General Loncar or General Lukic regarding protests sent by the Kosovo Verification Mission. The witness replied, I quote: "Instructions were given sometimes if he needed an answer, but there were never any reprimands." 19th March 2007, at page 11856, line 18 through 25, and page 11857, line 1 through 8. Let us say something at this point about paragraph 46(j). The Prosecutor alleges here that Sainovic expressed his view that a better balance of Serb and Albanian demographic levels should be achieved in Kosovo. The Prosecutor probably expected General Klaus Naumann to say something about this, but General Klaus Naumann didn't say anything about that. Furthermore, when the Defence asked him whether he remembered who had said at one of the meetings that Yugoslavia would have problems because of the Albanian birth-rate, General Naumann responded, I quote: "As far as I can remember, I don't know who exactly said that." 14th of December, 2006, at page 8374, lines 24 and 25. On the same occasion, General Naumann said that on the basis of intelligence available to NATO, the coordination between the military and the police was done in Nis and Belgrade. That's at page 8367, lines 20 through 23. This claim was confirmed by Colonel Crosland when the Defence asked the question at page 9870. It is quite easy to draw the conclusion from this that the coordination issues can have nothing to do with Sainovic, and as you can see we are talking about NATO intelligence. In paragraphs 47(c) -- (k), and 48 of the indictment, it is alleged that Sainovic exercised command authority and/or effective control over the units of the Yugoslav Army and MUP. It is also alleged that he had de facto authority over the highest-ranking officials in the Yugoslav Army and MUP. In paragraph 47(k) of the indictment and paragraph 401 of the Prosecution pre-trial brief, it is alleged that Sainovic had the power over the local authorities in Kosovo and over the interim Executive Council. So he had all the power he could in his hands, and this is completely untrue. There is nothing in the record to show that this was so, even in the interviews given to the Prosecution in this case. And let us use General Vasiljevic's evidence to prove the -- quite the opposite. That's the only witness who testified about the state of war period, when the state of war was in force. At page 8827, lines 8 to 20, Vasiljevic recounts a conversation at Slobodan Milosevic's in May 1999, when a discussion went on in order to establish the exact situation in Kosovo, and that to this end a supervisor should be sent there, either an individual or a group of people, and it is quite clear from Vasiljevic -- from what Vasiljevic said that Sainovic was not the supervisor in question, which can lead us to a conclusion that Sainovic had no powers that the Prosecutor alleges he had, because if it had been otherwise why would then a supervisor be needed in Kosovo? As regards paragraph 49 of the indictment, this is the mens rea, the requisite mens rea for the liability under Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the ICTY's Tribunal Statute. The Defence has already presented facts that bring into doubt the existence of the factors that might be the foundation of Nikola Sainovic's mens rea in relation to the alleged crimes; crimes that either happened or are alleged to have happened. The Prosecution also mentions alleged crimes from 1998. What crimes are these? Who has proven and in what case that there were crimes in 1998 that Sainovic was supposed to be notified of? What crimes was Sainovic notified of as a member of several FRY delegations charged with finding facts in Kosovo in 1998, and how, in what way? In order for us to be able to conclude reliably that crimes did happen. In relation to this paragraph, we have to stress that there is the difference between the events and players in 1998 and in 1999. The Prosecution keeps overlooking this difference. Prosecution witnesses do not, in fact, support the existence of the requisite mens rea of Nikola Sainovic for a liability under Article 7(1) and 7(3). Yet, Prosecution witnesses do provide us with elements for the determination of Nikola Sainovic's mens rea in 1998 and in the first few months of 1999. These witnesses give a very detailed and direct account of Nikola Sainovic's mens rea, but their description has nothing to do with what the Prosecution tried to paint in documents made before the evidence was actually adduced. So what I'm talking about is the indictment and the pre-trial brief. Thus, Ambassador Wolfgang Petritsch said that Sainovic was cooperative in his attitude towards international negotiators, and that this is how he remembered him. 2nd March 2007, at page 10945, lines 14 through 24. Witness Michael Phillips testified that, I quote: "Sainovic was sincere about trying to find some kind of a strategy for the co-existence of the Serb and Albanian population." That was on 19th of March, 2007, at page 11887, lines 9 through 11. Finally, Witness Shaun Byrnes fully supported the conclusion that Mr. Sainovic was cooperative at meetings with him, and that he did not engage in propaganda and was not prone to making any vehement speeches of any kind. That's 16th of April, 2007, at page 12188, lines 6 through 9. The Defence requests the Trial Chamber respectfully to find in relation to all these subparagraphs in paragraph 46, that's (a) through (j), or at least to some parts of this paragraph, to find that the Defence does not need to adduce any evidence to show that they are unsupported. The Defence also respectfully requests the Trial Chamber to find that all the paragraphs -- subparagraphs in paragraphs 47, 48, and 49, or at least major parts of these paragraphs, that the Defence does not have to adduce any evidence to show that they are unsupported. In some of the allegations the Prosecution made in the pre-trial brief, before the pre-trial phase, that the JCE hails back to times before the month of October 1998. It is alleged, for instance, that in June 1998, the political, military, and security elite of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia was divided into two camps: One camp advocating a political solution, and the second one - and Nikola Sainovic allegedly sided with them - advocated a military solution. There is no evidence of that in the record. In the same vein, it is alleged by the Prosecution that Sainovic said that the balance between Serbs and Albanians in Kosovo must be achieved, expressing his concern about the fact that the birth-rate among Albanians was higher than the birth-rate among Serbs. There is no evidence about that in the record. And as I already noted, Klaus Naumann testified otherwise. Of particular interest is the argument that Sainovic took part in obstructing negotiations with the Kosovo Albanians, and that he undermined the efforts to achieve a peaceful settlement for the Kosovo crisis through negotiations. Ambassador Petritsch and Mr. Byrnes say that Sainovic did all he could in order to achieve the exchange of prisoners. Byrnes says that the issue of the exchange of prisoners was of particular importance for him as the head of the American KDOM, and that the awareness of the importance of this exchange was something that he shared with Sainovic. He even remembers that Sainovic considered that a successful exchange should be a foundation for further efforts to stabilise the situation, as has already been said. It is also alleged that Sainovic directly obstructed and undermined those negotiations. Let us recall what Ambassador Petritsch and Mr. Byrnes said about Sainovic's role in Rambouillet. Not only did Sainovic not obstruct the negotiations, but Prosecution witnesses describe Sainovic as a sincere and committed negotiator who firmly believes in a political solution that would be acceptable to both parties. All those things that the Prosecutor states or alleges about efforts to obstruct the investigations and conceal the crimes in the documents drafted before the trial simply have nothing to do in any of their elements with what Nikola Sainovic did or the role he played. No evidence adduced before this Trial Chamber indicates that by his acts or omissions Sainovic contributed to the concealment of the crimes that had been committed and the impunity for those crimes. Nikola Sainovic's role in the events in 1998 and 1999, the way that the Prosecutor tried to paint it, is completely erroneous. Nikola Sainovic was the deputy prime minister in the federal government. The events in Kosovo found him as the deputy prime minister charged with foreign policy and international relations. At that time, the deterioration of the overall situation in Kosovo required all the state organs to step-up their activities within their constitutional and legal powers in order to try to find a settlement for the crisis that threatened to destabilise the whole country and the region. And such activities needed to be carried out in the spheres of defence, security, foreign policy, education, health care, and other -- in other spheres. The defence of the country, including the command and control over the VJ, was within the remit of the Supreme Defence Council. The internal affairs, education, health care, local self government, and other activities were within the remit of the organs and institutions of the Republic of Serbia. In 1998, the federal government had full authority over the -- overrunning the foreign policy of the country. The deterioration of the situation in Kosovo required the federal government to step-up its activity in foreign affairs. In March 1998, the OSCE decided to strengthen their observation teams from the missions accredited in Belgrade in order to be able to establish what the situation was in Kosovo. That's Exhibit 1D18 at page 289. After the -- after the agreement achieved between President Milosevic and President Yeltsin on the 16th of June, 1998, guarantying unimpeded access to international observers to the entire territory - that's Exhibit 1D18, page 289 - the number of international representatives in Kosovo grew exponentially. The international presence of this kind required an increased activity of the federal government in Kosovo in terms of foreign policy. This is how this decision was made to dispatch Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic to Kosovo as the deputy prime minister in charge of international affairs and -- international relations and foreign affairs. After political consultations, Federal Prime Minister Momir Bulatovic concludes that Nikola Sainovic should on behalf of the federal government be involved directly in Kosovo in the sphere of foreign affairs bearing in mind two facts: A, Nikola Sainovic's duties within the government; and B, the powers and the apparatus of the federal government in existence in the province. Within the framework of the activities of the federal government in Kosovo, Sainovic was involved in activities in foreign policy, including contacts with foreign diplomatic representatives and international organisations that had flocked to Kosovo in 1998 in large numbers. In June 1998, or to be more specific on the 10th of June, 1998, at a session of the SPS, the socialist party of Serbia, the ruling party headed by Slobodan Milosevic, their main board, this is Prosecution Exhibit P1012, and in order to step-up the activities in Kosovo itself, a decision was made to establish a team composed of prominent members of the SPS Main Board to go to Pristina and to assist in the implementation of the activities of the state organs geared to stabilise the situation in the province. This team comprised Zoran Andjelkovic, the -- a minister in the Republic of Serbia government; Dusko Matkovic, the envoy of the republic and a prominent businessman; and it was headed by Milomir Minic, the president of the Chamber of citizens of the FRY Assembly. This then debunks the myth called by the Prosecutor Joint Command. Representatives of the federal government and representatives of the ruling party were sent to Kosovo in order to assist in stabilising the situation in the region, each within his own sphere of competence. The government of the Republic of Serbia in the course of 1998 sent a large number of representatives from various ministries to intensify and coordinate the activities falling under their portfolios in Kosovo directly. When the verification mission of the OSCE arrived in Kosovo and Metohija, the federal government established a commission for cooperation with the mission. Nikola Sainovic was appointed by the federal government as the president of that commission, and that is Defence Exhibit 2D8. Witness -- Prosecution Witness Dusan Loncar also testified to this. The role of the commission was to assist and harmonise the activities of the federal government and the various ministries in implementing the agreement with the OSCE. The commission worked in compliance with the rules of procedure of the federal government which regulated the founding and functioning of ad hoc working bodies, and this can be concluded on the basis of this Defence exhibit. Nikola Sainovic never belonged to Milosevic's inner circle or, as the Prosecutor terms it, shadow cabinet. Moreover, in the relevant time-period, Sainovic was bereft of any important role in the ruling party in Serbia at the time. Although at the congress of the SPS in 1996, he was elected vice-president of that party; in 1997, he was dismissed from that post, and that was the situation in the ensuing years. We had prepared an exhibit to show Zoran Lilic to prove this; however, we will have to adduce it later on at a later stage of the proceedings. Any other interpretation of the role and place of Sainovic is at odds with all the evidence presented so far and also at odds with the truth. Let me now come to my conclusion. The Trial Chamber knows that the Defence of Sainovic has always done its best to expedite the proceedings and make them more efficient. Therefore, on this occasion also, Sainovic's Defence wishes to be efficient and innovative. Therefore, we move that the Trial Chamber, under Rule 98 bis, issue a decision stating that the Prosecution has failed to prove the following contentions and that the Sainovic Defence does not have to adduce any evidence to disprove them. First, that Nikola Sainovic was the commander of the Joint Command for Kosovo at the relevant time-period; two, that Nikola Sainovic and other civilians and politicians were members of the Joint Command in the course of 1999, if such a body existed at all; three, that Nikola Sainovic had real or formal powers to carry out investigations and to punish the perpetrators of crimes; four, that Nikola Sainovic had the authority and ability to control and command units of the army and police in 1999. Most of the Defence case will be devoted to proving these submissions. The trial would be greatly expedited and made much more efficient should the Trial Chamber establish that these contentions have not been proved by the Prosecution or that at least some of them have not been proved. The indictment against Sainovic also contains a so-called factual context. This contains a number of allegations which are supposed to represent the general context of the events, and in the view of the Defence, they have remained unproved. This pertains especially to the connection between the accused Sainovic with what is stated there. For example, in paragraph 88 of the indictment, there is mention of discrimination against Kosovo Albanians in education, in interior affairs, in the economy, in social policy. No evidence has been adduced by the Prosecution to show any kind of connection or role played by Sainovic in these processes. For this reason, the Defence asks or moves that the Chamber establish that there is no nexus between the processes described in paragraph 88 of the indictment and the accused Sainovic. This would save a great deal of time in the presentation of the Sainovic Defence case because should this not occur, the Defence will have to deal with all these issues, including education, health care, and other issues. Finally, the Prosecutor should answer the following question: If everything is the way the Defence says, why was one of the five deputy prime ministers separated out and accused in this case? The answer to that is simple: There are -- there were numerous meetings and numerous activities on the international level in which Nikola Sainovic participated, from the implementation of the Dayton Agreement to the Kosovo crisis. In the testimony of all the witnesses who have been heard here, it follows that Sainovic dealt with political issues, that he advocated a political solution to the crisis in Kosovo, that he advocated co-existence in Kosovo, and that he did not hesitate to meet even representatives of the KLA, or rather, he did not hesitate to express the desire to meet representatives of the KLA, only in order to achieve this goal. In Rambouillet, Sainovic together with Ratko Markovic managed to achieve an agreement about the political part of the agreement. Everything Sainovic did was to work on political issues, those he was tasked with. And everything he did was simply his patriotic duty as a politician who was committed to finding a political solution to the crisis. Sainovic's activity and commitment to his job made him prominent enough for some malicious people to think that the key of the Kosovo enigma was to a large extent in his hands. The Defence wonders whether Sainovic who, as all the witnesses, foreign diplomats and others, have said, worked for peace, advocated a multi-ethnic Kosovo, accepted the political agreement in Rambouillet, and for all these reasons was marginalised in the negotiations in Paris and no longer participated in negotiations at Milosevic's, as Ambassador Petritsch testifies, should now be found guilty of serious crimes because of all these things. I wish to refer to a Latin saying which was the basis for the presentation of evidence in Roman times: "Tetis unus, tetis nullus." This means it is not enough to have one witness in order to establish something; that one witness equals no witnesses. The Romans were referring, of course, to eye-witnesses, to first-hand evidence. The Prosecution has brought forward witnesses with only hearsay, second-hand knowledge or even fourth-hand knowledge, as in the case of Tanic. If the Romans said that one eye-witness equals zero witnesses, then these witnesses amount to four zeros, depending on how far removed they are from the evidence. The Defence wishes to say -- to raise another point in relation to witnesses. This process will end with some kind of judgement which will not deal only with the criminal aspects of the case. This is a historical proceeding because inevitably it also deals with political issues, such as the negotiations in Rambouillet, the negotiations preceding Rambouillet, the reasons for the air-strikes against a sovereign country without the approval of the United Nations - and this is the United Nations Tribunal - and after we all leave this place, this judgement will be studied for a long time to come. In order to reach such a decision, much more should have been done by the Prosecution than has been done. I'm personally satisfied that I had the honour to have as my legal opponents Mr. Hannis, Mr. Stamp, and Mr. Marcussen, and it was even -- an even greater honour to meet the more charming and beautiful part of their team, but - and there is always a but - the selection of witnesses and documents for this historical proceeding was, in my view, not up to the mark. For the Tribunal to hand down such a historical decision without ever having all this work brought into question, I expected to see at least an attempt to call as witnesses, for example, Generals Momcilo Perisic, Aca Dimitrijevic, Geza Farkas from the Army of Yugoslavia, then at least one general from the collegium of General Ojdanic and most especially a military analyst. Then from the MUP of Serbia, Jovica Stanisic, Frenki Simatovic, Obrad Stevanovic, Dragan Ilic, and most importantly a police analyst. From among the politicians, Milo Djukanovic, who is now a businessman in Podgorica, but who was once one of the three members of the Supreme Defence Council. One of them is deceased, another one is sitting right behind me, while the third is engaged in business, and his testimony would have been very valuable, not only with reference to the VSO but also in -- with reference to meetings with Ambassadors Walker and so on. Momir Bulatovic, who I hope to call; Zivadin Jovanovic, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the FRY. Zivadin Jovanovic, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the FRY, whom I will also attempt to call; Vladan Kutlesic, the special envoy of Slobodan Milosevic for Kosovo; and Deputy Prime Minister, whom I cannot call and don't want to call, Ratko Markovic, the Deputy Prime Minister of the Serbian government, the author of the Serbian constitution, and the head of the delegation in Rambouillet and also in Kosovo in negotiations with Rugova; Bojan Bugarcic, Milosevic's advisor for foreign policy who negotiated with Petritsch after Rambouillet, and an expert for constitutional issues of the FRY who would testify to the relation between the federal state and the member republics. And finally, witnesses from abroad, primarily Mr. Christopher Hill and Ambassador Boris Mayorski, who, together with Ambassador Petritsch, were the three negotiators in Rambouillet; Ambassador then Geremek; Ambassador Keller; Bo Pelinas and others. It is still not impossible to do this, applying Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Crime base witnesses have a limited value because they are only victims. Of course, they have the right to our compassion, our understanding, but that's as far as they go. Second-hand testimony, where national legislation is accepted as a necessary evil if -- are accepted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] National legislations accept hearsay testimony mainly as a necessary evil in cases where there are no eye-witnesses, no first-hand witnesses, but this Defence wishes to show that there are such witnesses but that insufficient efforts were made or there was not the will to call them here. Had the witnesses I have enumerated been called, this Tribunal would have had credible witnesses and would have been able to hand down a truly historical judgement. I say this with regret, not because I have any malicious intentions. Finally, I wish to thank you for your time and attention, and it is time for me to put forward my final proposal. Looking at the evidence presented against Nikola Sainovic as a whole, the Defence feels that it has not been proved that he is guilty under any of the five counts of the indictment, and therefore the Defence moves that the Trial Chamber hand down an acquittal for Sainovic in accordance with Rule 98 bis, applying the principle of in dubio pro reo, which is one of the fundamental principles of law. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify one thing. You've said that the -- you made a comparison between crime base witnesses and those who were victims. Now, can you kindly elaborate on that? I mean, crime base witnesses and witnesses you thought were ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. In my view, it's all the same, but they cannot be useful for the Trial Chamber to determine the broader truth, aside from what happened to them and their kin. So this is why I say that their evidentiary value is limited, because they always testify about one single event, no matter how horrible it is, but what you need in order to see the broader truth, you have to see the whole range of events, what was happening in the world at that time and who were the real players who brought all this about. And that is why we could perhaps understand finally why a country is brought in a situation where it is about to lose one of its constituent parts, which is what we are facing now. So this is the difference that I'm talking about. I'm talking about crime base witnesses. The only thing that is at issue here is whether this witness is telling the truth or not, but it is not useful for the broader picture. I hope that now I've explained this to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Of course, there is a duty on the Defence in that respect to point out where things have been omitted and where truth have been suppressed and to complete the picture, if that is possible, if something has been oppressed, and we expect that you would be able to assist us in that direction, but you haven't pointed out anything. Maybe this is not the stage maybe, at 98. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, we're not at this stage indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, part of that discussion just now was about the possibility that there may be some contradiction between your acceptance of what Mr. O'Sullivan has said on the law, on the test for 98 bis, and your reference latterly to the question of proof beyond reasonable doubt. My own view was that what you were saying was that the quality of this evidence -- not so much the quality, but the nature of some of the evidence being hearsay evidence rather than eye-witness evidence, being from a limited number of people when there were more available, was such that it was not capable of entitling the Chamber to make a finding of guilt. Is that what you were saying about the various -- in your latter submissions about the omissions to lead certain evidence by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would not like to move beyond the framework of 98 bis, and that is the reason why I didn't go that far. And the reason why I made this criticism is because the evidence was simply not up to the mark at this trial, and I noticed some lack of willingness as, for instance, on the part of the US government to place at our disposal some documents when, for instance, they refused to provide documents indicating where there are -- air-strikes actually were, and I tried to obtain this evidence. I even tried to do so in collaboration with the Prosecution, but we failed. And that is why I wanted to have these people that I listed here because the weight of your judgement would be that much greater because of that. Because the main criticism levied at this Tribunal in the world is because people are saying, Well, Tom said this to Bill, Bill said this to Jim, and this is then admitted as evidence. This is the criticism that is levied. And I think that simply the quantity of evidence is insufficient. This is what I said in the pre-trial stage, and I didn't really change my opinion. This is the thing that I wanted to note. And the hearsay evidence that was adduced is insufficient for this Trial Chamber to find the -- that there is enough evidence against the accused, even hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm now trying -- I've now tried to expand a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. The position is clearer now. Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And may it please the Court, it's my privilege today, together with Mr. Visnjic, to represent General Ojdanic in support of his motion for a judgement of acquittal. General Ojdanic personally addressed you at the beginning of the trial and told you that he never participated in any joint criminal enterprise to expel Albanians from Kosovo, and that he took all reasonable and necessary steps to prevent and punish crimes in Kosovo. As I stand here before you some ten months later, we respectfully submit that the evidence has shown that what General Ojdanic told you was true. I have a duty at this point in the case to resist the advocate's temptation to construe and argue the evidence in a light most favourable to General Ojdanic. As a matter of fact, my duty is to the contrary, and I recognise that. I have a duty at this point, under 98 bis, to construe the evidence in the light most favourable to the Prosecution, and I recognise, of course, that a Trial Chamber can uphold a Rule 98 bis motion only if it is entitled to conclude that no reasonable trier of fact could find the evidence sufficient to sustain a conviction beyond a reasonable doubt. And that, indeed, is our submission to you today, that no reasonable trier of fact could find General Ojdanic guilty beyond a reasonable doubt on this record. I'm going to spend most of my time allotment discussing the evidence from the date that General Ojdanic became chief of the army's General Staff in late November 1998. But I think it important to first discuss an event that took place some three months before on August 27th, 1998, and that is the briefing that General Ojdanic gave on that day to military attaches in Belgrade, a meeting attended by Colonel John Crosland. And before getting to that meeting, I want to briefly recall for the Trial Chamber the evidence which showed during various times in 1998 that the MUP, acting alone, was not always able to adequately deal with KLA acts and provocations. One example of that is in Podujevo, which I will discuss shortly. But the plain fact is that as early as July 1998, General Perisic, then the army's Chief of Staff, recognising the military necessity, issued a directive in which he stated, and I quote: "Through its presence and by carrying out training in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the army has had a repelling effect with regard to the Siptar Albanian terrorist forces and it has offered direct assistance to the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia." That's 4D137, page 2. In that same directive of 28 July 1998, General Perisic further stated that the Yugoslav Army: "Has intensified the security for military facilities and units in Kosovo and Metohija, and it ensured a regular supply flow to the Yugoslav Army units for the execution of their tasks." That's again 4D137 at page 2. These statements of General Perisic in his 28 July 1998 directive were simply echoed by General Ojdanic as the Deputy Chief of Staff when he made his comments on 27 August 1998 to the military attaches in Belgrade at a meeting attended by, among others, Colonel Crosland. In his report of 28 August 1998, Colonel Crosland reported as follows, and this is 3D512, he said: "Ojdanic outlined four tasks of VJ and explained VJ wider deployment in Kosovo was in order to protect lines of communications which the MUP could not do -- could not do." He went on to say: "These routes had been and were now subject to guerilla-type attacks, and this task was therefore difficult to implement." In addition to protecting lines of communication, General Ojdanic mentioned three other VJ tasks: To maintain border security; to protect VJ installations; and to protect VJ units, both in barracks and in the field. The Trial Chamber will recall that Colonel Crosland agreed that the four main tasks of the VJ announced by General Ojdanic at the briefing made imminently good military sense. Citing General Ojdanic's statement at the briefing conference that force would be met with force, Colonel Crosland agreed that the VJ-MUP could, of course, use appropriate but not disproportionate force to respond to KLA attacks and provocations. In a perfect world, that should have been the end of the August 27, 1998, briefing story and we could move on. But I respectfully suggest to you that we can't really do that because Colonel Crosland in repeated statements to the Office of the Prosecutor over several years and in his direct trial testimony here stated as follows, and I'll quote from his statement, which is P2645, paragraph 49: "The constitutional change to the role of the VJ was shortly after I showed the Deputy Chief of the General Staff Ojdanic a video in August 1998, proving that the VJ was involved in internal security operations, something he had denied." Well, of course, we now know that that was an erroneous statement. Colonel Crosland, after much backing and filling, finally admitted on cross-examination that he did not show this video to General Ojdanic or even hand it to him personally at any time. The Trial Chamber may recall that in confronting Colonel Crosland about the alleged showing of the video, I said - and I'm quoting now: "I respectfully submit to you, sir, that I think you're wrong about that, just like you were wrong about Lord Ashdown." And I'll say here parenthetically you'll recall that Colonel Crosland admitted to Ms. Carter, Prosecutor Carter, the day before he testified, that he and Lord Ashdown had never shown photographic evidence to General Ojdanic of the VJ shelling Suva Reka in September 1998, as he also erroneously said in paragraph 51 of his statement and, indeed, had erroneously so testified in the Milosevic trial. And continuing on with the cross-examination, my cross-examination of Colonel Crosland, I said: "And by the way, sitting here now -- sitting here now before I get into my questions, are you prepared to concede if I make a sufficient demonstration to you that you got that wrong, too?" In other words, in addition to Lord Ashdown, that you've also gotten this wrong, that in fact you never really showed this video to General Ojdanic. And the answer was: "No. I represent, as I've said, the video was given to the Vojska Jugoslavije. Whether General Ojdanic or anyone else looked at it, I have no idea. "Q. So you didn't show this video to General Ojdanic on August 27th, 1998? "A. I presented it to him or his staff, and what they did with it, I do not know. "Q. I presented it to him or his staff? There's a difference. There's a difference, sir. Who did you present it to? "A. I think at the time -- I think at the time Colonel Negovan Jovanovic, who was the head of the foreign liaison service, was at this meeting and I probably gave it to him. "Q. So sitting here right now, is it fair to say you have no idea whether General Ojdanic ever viewed that video? "A. I've told you that, sir. It was not my job to ask the general to look at a video because in my army, you would be put in clank." Now, what is the practical importance of all this to our case, aside from showing that this portion of Colonel Crosland's OTP statement and direct testimony was not true? I suggest that it shows that even a witness with the credentials of Colonel Crosland can get it badly wrong, can have a mindset which closes out other possibilities, and can result, if not discovered as it was fortunately -- as it was fortunately here, can result in a miscarriage of justice. At the least it shows the frailty and fallibility of human memory, something that is traditionally tested in cross-examination. But what makes this situation even more disturbing - at least in my view, it is disturbing, and I hope in the view of the Trial Chamber, it's disturbing - is that my cross-examination had little, if anything, to do with getting at the truth of this. As Judge Bonomy aptly observed on this point during cross-examination, speaking to me, he said: "You've got to something you might not have discovered, and you may have reached it by accident." That's transcript 9892. Well, Judge Bonomy was exactly right, and that shows how fragile our system of justice can be and why it's so important to keep getting it right. And as we go along, I'm going to point out other areas where I firmly believe that the OTP has not gotten it right, how the OTP, indeed, has also this erroneous mindset about General Ojdanic that I've referred to and why this motion for judgement of acquittal should be granted. I'd like to continue our discussion of the evidence with General Ojdanic's appointment as Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army on 24 November 1998. In his opening statement, Mr. Hannis said this about the appointment of General Ojdanic to replace General Perisic and other appointments at the same time. Mr. Hannis said: "The evidence supports the suggestion that the new faces were seen as individuals who were willing to follow the course intended by Milosevic in terms of solving in spring 1999 the Kosovo problem, the Kosovo problem being ethnic imbalance." That's page 430 of the 10 July transcript. This statement of Mr. Hannis is simply wrong and not at all supported by the evidence. Ironically enough, in the light of Mr. Hannis's comments, when General Ojdanic took charge of the collegium of the General Staff, this is what he had to say to his colleagues on 27 November 1998: "To what extent I am a hard-liner, how blind or loyal I am, my position on resolving the problems in Kosovo and Metohija, I hope you know and are witnesses of my participation in the meetings of the collegium, if nothing else. Rest assured that in your colleague, who has been given the difficult task of leading you, you have a man who above all thinks with his own head and is his own man. This is how I've been and I remain so, and I have no intention to nor can I change this at this very late stage in my career." And you'll find that at Exhibit P925 at page 9. Now, I'm going to suggest to you, and this suggestion is strongly based on the evidence, that General Ojdanic was, indeed, his own man and made decisions solely on the basis of what he thought was right. The evidence is going to show in this case -- and maybe you caught some of the flavour of that when he made his little statement to you at the beginning, the evidence is going to show a person who is up-front, what you see is what you get, he says what he means, he means what he says. He's without guile; he's without duplicity. And I'm confident that the collegiums, a number of which you're going to hear about today, will bear this out and will bear out these qualities of General Ojdanic. You may recall that for three years, General Ojdanic and his Defence team -- and his Defence team at that time was -- was Mr. Visnjic and Mr. Robinson, Peter Robinson, his Defence team fought to get evidence from NATO and its member states of intercepted conversations which would show General Ojdanic's words and deeds, and his innocent state of mind. In the end, they unfortunately didn't have such intercepts, but the verbatim transcripts of the collegium are the next best thing providing you with an opportunity to understand what, why, and how General Ojdanic conducted himself during the events in issue in this case. We have 25 collegiums in evidence in this case; 22 of them from 27 November 1998 to 9 April 1999; and three prior to 27 November 1998. The transcript of these collegium meetings represent spontaneous, contemporaneous, and frank discussions of the General Staff concerning the very issues which are the subject of this trial. The collegiums show frequent, intense, and high-spirited discussions among generals. These are men with strong views, who are not afraid to express their opinions. I hope you'll be impressed, as I was, by the range and cogency of these discussions and note that there were frequently doubts expressed as to the best and wisest policy to be pursued. I hope you will also note that virtually without exception the comments and decisions made by General Ojdanic were always to resolve doubts in favour of openness and candour and truth. I say this with full confidence, and I say it now since I'll have no right to reply to what Mr. Hannis might say about these collegiums. I respectfully submit to you that the collegiums, when read in their entirety and not just a little snippet that Mr. Hannis read during the re-direct examination of Mr. Byrnes, when read in their entirety, these collegiums are the key to demonstrating that there was no plan to expel Kosovar Albanians, and the key to determining General Ojdanic's personal responsibility in this case. And I urge you to pay great attention to them in your deliberation on these motions. Before --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly requested to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm requested to read more slowly, and I promise to try to abide by that. By my likes, Your Honour, I'm actually creeping, believe it or not, and so I will make even further efforts to slow down. Mr. Visnjic has probably passed me 20 notes that I'm going too quickly, but I apologise if I slow down too much. So before turning to the collegiums, which start for our purposes on 27 November 1998, three days after General Ojdanic became Chief of Staff, I want to put my discussion in the context of what was going on in Kosovo at that time. It's particularly important to do this, since the Prosecution in its indictment alleges that the joint criminal enterprise came into existence no later than October 1998 and continued until 20 June 1999. Now, what was happening in late 1998 when General Ojdanic became Chief of the General Staff? We know from the evidence that Serbian forces following their summer offensive against the KLA had succeeded in recapturing most of the territory previously occupied by the KLA. United Nations Security Council Resolution 1199 called for a cease-fire and resolution of the conflict between -- that was taking place. To this end, the Clark-Naumann-Milosevic Agreement was reached on 25 October 1998. It called for the reduction of VJ and MUP forces to February/March 1998 levels. We know from the evidence what happened after that. As General Naumann, General DZ, Colonel Crosland, and others testified, the Serbian side honoured its commitments and withdrew their forces. The KLA then filled the void left by these forces, oozed back into these areas as one observer put it. And as the KLA Chief of Staff Bislim Zyrapi stated, this is the report of 28 December 1998, P2460: "Following the enemy offensive, the repositioning of forces has been carried out in all operating zones, and we can freely say that the territory controlled by our units is now a greater percentage than prior to the enemy offensive." To complete the picture of what General Ojdanic was facing when he became Chief of Staff, the Trial Chamber will recall the very significant evidence that starting in late 1998, and continuing right until the start of the war in March 1999, KLA terrorist attacks and provocations continued and, indeed, escalated in violation of the cease-fire. The evidence is overwhelming on this point. General Naumann: "In most cases the escalation came from the Kosovo side, not the Serb side." 3D377. Ambassador Walker, as stated in notes recorded by Colonel Phillips of 30 November 1998, and I quote: "Most of the violent acts are being committed by the KLA." 3D564. General DZ: "I must say that during the Rambouillet discussions, the number of incidents instigated by the Serbs declined significantly, whereas those instigated by the KLA declined much less appreciably. Furthermore, the KLA became more opportunistic during this time." P2508, paragraph 189. General DZ, March 1st, 1999, in his notebook: "KLA actions on the ground are becoming increasingly unrestrained. The return of the KLA leadership from France on 25 February does not appear to have affected the situation for the good. KLA have taken hostages in the Prizren region in the latest incident in a spade of detentions by the KLA. There has also been KLA activity around Kacanik, an area which has been quiet in recent months." 3D573, page 32. Moreover, a series of reports and assessments made by the Kosovo Verification Mission were to the same effect. I certainly won't mention them all. You've heard extensive evidence about this. Just one example is a KVM report covering the period 23 February to 11 March 1999, 3D179, which states that: "Unprovoked attacks by the KLA against the police have continued, and the number of casualties sustained by the security forces has increased." The report goes on to say that incidents of kidnapping and abductions by the KLA have continued. And the Chamber will recall the various ambushes and killings of policemen. The murder of six Serb teenagers in the Panda Bar in Pec; the kidnapping and killing of the deputy mayor of Kosovo Polje; the killing of both Serb civilians and so-called Albanian collaborators continuing right up until the war started, one of the last recorded incidents being on 21 March 1999 when four members of the MUP were shot and killed in a KLA ambush in Pristina. In its comment to the report by the KVM fusion centre, the report states that this is the first urban attack against the MUP in Pristina, and the Trial Chamber will recall the testimony of Colonel Phillips that the KLA had targeted for attack other urban areas aside from Pristina. Transcript of 20 March 2007 at pages 1215 and 1216. So by the beginning of the war on March 23rd, 1999, the KLA had transformed itself, as Bislim Zyrapi testified, from a popular guerilla army to a more effective organised army of some 17 to 18.000 men combined with, when necessary, the use of hit-and-run guerilla tactics and generally supported by a large majority of the Albanian population. On the question of KLA numbers, I suggest that the most authoritative source is Commander Zyrapi for obvious reasons, but the fact is the KLA membership as set forth in an ECMM memorandum of June 22, 1998, that's P2136, was almost unlimited. This report, a good part of which was read to you during the cross-examination of Colonel Crosland - and I won't read it again, but I do commend it to you, the report makes the following conclusion: "The larger family unit to which an Albanian so often derives support is still the most plausible overall structure on which the UCK is attached and will remain their greatest strength. In this way, membership of the UCK becomes unlimited." Even Colonel Crosland, who put the hard-core number of KLA fighters at 400, another erroneous mindset of Colonel Crosland, I respectfully suggest, even Colonel Crosland agreed with the ECMM assessment and stated: "It was entirely in line with what I've told you on the bigger picture of the KLA and the potential for major numbers to appear." Transcript 9905. Indeed, in his OTP statement of June 30, 2006, 3D510, at paragraph 49, Colonel Crosland states that: "I think that the clan-based society, that is Kosovo, actually made the KLA stronger. You need the tacit support of the whole family to get involved, but once you had it, everyone would support the cause." And then finally, to complete the picture of the difficulties posed by the -- by the KLA and what was facing General Ojdanic when he became the Chief of the General Staff, we have the observation of Colonel Crosland made in a meeting of 25 June 1998 with Colonel Jovanovic, who was serving as a liaison to the foreign military representatives. Colonel Jovanovic's report on this meeting, 3D511, was confirmed as accurate by Colonel Crosland in his testimony at 9909 through 12. The report summarises Colonel Crosland's views on the KLA, including: "That the KLA is increasingly revealing its fundamental characteristic as a terrorist organisation which has no qualms in liquidating its members for the slightest disobedience. Something that has become more apparent recently." Colonel Crosland further states: "The situation is also rendered more complex by the fact that in Kosovo-Metohija, there is no front line separating the two opposing forces, but instead there are terrorist groups which set up base mostly in settled places with an ethnically pure population supportive of the idea of Kosovo a republic." So those were the harsh realities facing General Ojdanic both when he assumed command of the General Staff in late November 1998 and continuing to the start of the war. He had to ensure that the VJ fulfilled its responsibilities set forth in the October 25 Clark-Naumann Agreement and at the same time respond to the continuing threat posed by the actions and provocations of the KLA and the threat of bombing by NATO forces. How did he respond? We say honourably, decently, professionally, as the evidence shows. His first job was to deal with the Kosovo Verification Mission, and I submit to you that General Ojdanic's dealings with the KVM were honourable and straightforward, as the evidence clearly shows. Though new on the job on 27 November 1998, just three days after his appointment as Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic met with General DZ, the chief of operations for the KVM. As General DZ testified, General Ojdanic assured him that the VJ would fulfil all their obligations under the FRY-OSCE Agreement. General Ojdanic expressed the desire for transparent troop rotations in and out of Kosovo, which he said were a normal part of operations and should not be misunderstood by the international community. General DZ described General Ojdanic's attitude during this meeting as correct and confirmed that the KVM was indeed provided with the information promised by General Ojdanic two days later. You will find that testimony of General DZ at pages 7919 and 7923 of the transcript of 5 December 2006. General DZ further testified that his impression of the meeting with General Ojdanic was that the general had just given him the green light to open discussions with the lower levels of command, which was the whole purpose of the meeting, given that General Ojdanic had just assumed his position. That's at transcript 80 -- 88013-14 [sic]. General Ojdanic had agreed to transparent troop rotations at their initial meeting, as was clearly reflected in General DZ's contemporary notes taken about the meeting. 3D412, page 317. General DZ, however, claimed in his statement to the OTP and here at the trial in direct examination that his request to verify troop rotations was "refused by Ojdanic and refused with considerable authority," that's P2508, paragraph 66. The Trial Chamber may recall that I took strong issue with this testimony since I was convinced that it was incorrect, and I mentioned to General DZ on cross-examination, that his notes revealed no such conversation with General Ojdanic. I asked the general whether he was willing to concede that he may indeed have gotten this wrong. The Chamber may also recall that General DZ admitted that he may have gotten it wrong and that his present recollection was that it was General Loncar, as he put it "I'm pretty sure" it was General Loncar who communicated this alleged comment by General Ojdanic; that's TR7927. General DZ testified that he did not receive all the information he wanted as a KVM verifier, but it's clear from the evidence that this was not due to any action or decision of General Ojdanic. As General Loncar testified, "The army never interpreted international agreements; it simply implemented them, as instructed by the political authorities." That's transcript of 1 December 2006 at 7673. General DZ testified that he did not receive all the information he wanted because of the difference of interpretation between the OSCE and the Serbian political leadership over what was required under the agreement. This is a subject open to debate, but the short of it is that General Ojdanic was acutely conscious of the army's obligations in this regard, and he went the last mile to fulfil them. And this is again confirmed by the collegiums, as we will now show. General Ojdanic expressed his attitude about cooperation with the newly formed Kosovo Verification Mission at his very first collegium as Chief of the General Staff. He said: "I personally think that every unit, every troop rotation we can and should report to the verifiers, and this will not cause any problems. This goes out, this comes in, rather than having accusing [sic] us of bringing in reinforcements given the situation we've been put in." You'll find this in Exhibit -- that Exhibit 925 at page 16, the transcript of the collegium of 27 November 1998. That was the same day that General Ojdanic, again new on the job, met with General DZ. In his comments to the collegium on 17 December 1998, General Ojdanic stated, and I summarize here, I summarize closely, though, based on wording: The members of the verifier group all have diplomatic status, and that is how they should be approached. There should be no forms of crudeness shown to them. This the least painless form of intrusion, and we should not give them a reason to withdraw. You'll find that in Exhibit 3D494, at page 21. General Ojdanic also sought to improve the army's cooperation with the verifiers. You'll recall the testimony of General Loncar that in December 1998, General Ojdanic issued an order improving the cooperation with OSCE by relieving liaison officers of other duties and submitting reports on a daily basis to OSCE. This testimony can be found in transcript of 1 December 2006, at pages 7675 and 7676. The order itself is Exhibit 3D408 at page 2. At the collegium of 24 December 1998, General Ojdanic reiterated - and I summarize here - all commanding levels should study the Security Council resolutions and agreements, and demand that they be strictly observed. Nobody in the army has a right to violate these agreements. And then quoting directly word for word: "Adventurism or false patriotism which results in wilful behaviour which goes against the resolutions or agreements must be severely sanctioned because such behaviour could have fatal consequences for both this country and its people." You'll find that at Exhibit 924 at page 27. Now, I've already referred to the evidence that while the army withdrew from Kosovo and attempted to comply with its international obligations, the KLA took advantage by filling in the positions, strengthening its forces, and threatening the local population. And that is exactly what happened in the Podujevo area in December of 1998. This led to the deployment of Yugoslavian Army personnel to the Podujevo area at the end of December, which was construed, as the Prosecution has submitted here, as a violation of the agreement. I want to spend a few minutes discussing the Podujevo situation, and I'm happy to continue to do it now, Your Honour, or I don't know whether -- I probably have at least another five to ten minutes on Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it might be convenient to break now and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd just gotten to the event that was happening in Podujevo in December of 1998, where the Kosovo Liberation Army had moved back into that area previously vacated by the Serb forces. And I want to spend some time discussing Podujevo, particularly to make it clear that the VJ was not in Podujevo to either harass or expel Kosovar Albanian citizens from the area. A unit of the VJ was in Podujevo in December 1998, I submit to you, for two very good reasons. One was to protect the Serbian civilian population, which, as both Colonel Phillips and Shaun Byrnes confirmed, were being terrorised and driven out of the area by substantial KLA forces. The rather desperate condition of the Serb civilians in the area was graphically described in Prosecution Exhibit 414, which is a letter to various government Serbian officials -- government officials in Serbia from two leading citizens of the Podujevo Municipal Assembly, which describes terrorist acts by a KLA that "have become so strong that they are marauding through the area literally armed to the teeth with automatic rifles, hand-held rocket-launchers, necklaces of hand-grenades and cartridge belts in the camouflage and black uniforms of what they call their police." You will recall the black uniformed police as described by Mr. Byrnes as "sinister" and headed by a man called Geza, who had a reputation for ruthlessness and for killing both Serb and Albanian citizens. In their plea for help, the letter includes a request: "That we again insist for the umpteenth time on the stationing of a Yugoslav Army garrison on the territory of our municipality." In addition to protecting civilians, the second reason for the VJ presence, again confirmed by Phillips and Byrnes, was that it was very important for both Serb forces and the military to keep open the very strategic road which connected traffic from Belgrade down to Podujevo to Pristina. So given these very good reasons for the presence of a VJ unit, what's the problem? The problem, as Mr. Byrnes testified, is that the VJ presence in Podujevo allegedly violated that portion of the October 1998 Clark-Naumann Agreement which only allowed three company-size units in Kosovo to protect three specified roads which did not include the Podujevo-Pristina road. The Trial Chamber will recall that General Loncar testified that in his opinion there was no violation of the agreement, since the army in Podujevo was not deployed for combat but was there on a training mission and specifically to train personnel to operate tanks. That's at pages 7623, 7630 of the record. Mr. Byrnes testified that calling this a training -- calling this a training mission was just an excuse, as he put it, to have a VJ unit in the area. You'll recall that Judge Bonomy asked Mr. Byrnes, and I quote: "Let's assume it was a genuine exercise, would it be permitted by the Agreement agreement?" Mr. Byrnes stated that his "recollection of the agreement is not so precise that I can answer that question directly." Well, I'm not sure I can answer Judge Bonomy's question either, based on the language of the agreement. We do know, however, from Ambassador Walker's letter to Mr. Milosevic on 23 November 1998, that's Prosecution Exhibit 396, that information required to be furnished by Serbian forces in Kosovo included: "Those security force sites at which no formation, unit, or subunit is located (for example, training areas)." So it's certainly a legitimate conclusion that training areas were indeed contemplated under the agreement, and why shouldn't a training area include an area where, as Mr. Byrnes testified, the KLA commander Remi was "very aggressive" and "was constantly pushing the envelope, if you will." This is aside from the fact that the October 25 Clark-Naumann Agreement - and that's P395 - retained for Serb authorities "the right to respond adequately and proportionately to any form of terrorist activity or violation of law which could jeopardise the lives and safety of citizens and representatives of the state authorities." Now, how did General Ojdanic and the General Staff react to the events in Podujevo? Again, the collegiums provide a compelling answer. The discussion at the collegium of 30 December 1998 demonstrates that a VJ unit was in the Podujevo area not as part of any effort or any plan to harass or expel Kosovo-Albanian citizens, but because it was necessary to protect Serb civilians and important convoy and supply routes. General Dimitrijevic reported that the KLA is in a position to block the Pristina-Podujevo road whenever they wish, and that the KLA actions have resulted in the abandonment of three Serb villages in the Podujevo area. He said that the entire state structure had left Podujevo, and it is only the army's pressure in Podujevo which is managing to ensure the safety of the remaining Serb civilians. You'll find that on pages 7 through 10 of Exhibit P928, again the minutes of the collegium of 30 December 1998. At that collegium, General Ojdanic justified the deployment of the army in the Podujevo area by recalling what General Perisic had said when he agreed to the condition of withdrawal of the VJ at an earlier time; that if the other side threatened the local population, we would be forced to bring this group back into the area. You'll find that at page 17 of Exhibit P928. Now, finally, on this question of whether this was an exercise, we'll recall -- the Chamber will recall the re-direct examination by Mr. Hannis of Mr. Byrnes, and Mr. Hannis referred Mr. Byrnes to that particular collegium I just quoted from, P928, and he had Mr. Byrnes read out the following from General Dimitrijevic's language. General Dimitrijevic said: "The explanation that this was a planned exercise, that is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do. The fact the MUP did not do what it had to do afterwards has resulted in what we have now." And then on re-cross-examination, I asked Mr. Byrnes to read again from the collegium. I was gently chided by Judge Bonomy for doing so, but I was trying to get this -- this into evidence for you. And at that time on page 17 of this particular collegium, Colonel -- General Ojdanic said -- here's what he said about Podujevo: "These claims presented here regarding the situation down there in and around Podujevo that the presence of this unit added to it, it was really a matter of whether the marching route and the location of the camp were selected correctly, but this unit really was bivouacked there. I was assured of this by the commander of the army"; the commander of the army at that time being General Samardzic. So we have General Dimitrijevic saying it's not an exercise; we have General Loncar and the 3rd Army commander saying that it is an exercise. Now, if we were at the end of the case and we were arguing the case, then I would invoke the principle in dubio pro reo and ask you to resolve doubts in favour of General Ojdanic, but we're not in that part of the case, and I concede that viewing this in the light most favourable to the Prosecution, you're entitled to conclude that this was not an exercise. But what does that say? All that shows, that at most this was a violation of the Clark-Naumann Agreement, but that's not what General Ojdanic is charged with. He's charged with being part of a joint criminal enterprise to deport Kosovo-Albanians. And in that regard, it's very clear from this meeting that the purpose -- very clear from the collegiums, that the purpose was not to do that but to protect Serbian civilians and to protect that very strategic road. And incidentally, again, other generals had a fair amount to say about this during that collegium, and it would really be instructive, I think, for the -- for the Trial Chamber to read the entire discussion that took place at that time. Now, continuing the chronology, we're now into January of 1999, and at that collegium on January 14th, 1999, it was reported that in the last week, measures were taken to ensure full implementation of the agreement with OSCE. The General Staff once again remarked that any failure of the OSCE monitoring admission [sic] could be used by those who support other kinds of engagement by international forces in Kosovo. You'll find that at pages 6 to 9 of Exhibit P936. In the next days, the event at Racak occurred. Now, again, we know that the Trial Chamber has eliminated Racak as a scene, a crime scene, in the indictment, but as you also well know, there have been all sorts of testimony about it on pattern, command, function, et cetera. And at the collegium on 21 January 1999, General Ojdanic was assured that the army was not involved in this incident. He told the collegium that he had ordered the corps command to provide a report of where the army units were and what they were doing. He reported that he studied the report in detail, and it represents the army was not involved and that no artillery support was given. General Ojdanic went on to say there is no reason to hide anything. If the army was involved, we'll admit it and take the consequences. "As the Chief of the General Staff, I want to know the truth." You'll find these comments at pages 10 and 12 of Exhibit P939. Throughout the remainder of January and February, as the political pressure from the international community mounted on the government, General Ojdanic and the General Staff continued to urge restraint so as not to provoke a NATO attack. You can see this in the collegium discussions on 2 February 1999, which is Exhibit 931 at page 6, and the collegium of 25 February 1999, which is Exhibit 941 at pages 5 through 7. In the collegium of 11 February 1999, General Ojdanic directed that the army's liaison officers with the Kosovo Verification Mission be upgraded, and that English-speaking officers be transferred to perform liaison duties. That's in Exhibit P934 at pages 24, 25, and then in the order he issued on 89 -- 8 March 1999, which is Exhibit 3D407. General Loncar also testified about this at pages 7677 and 7680. As the threats and military preparations from the international community intensified during February and March 1999, General Ojdanic and the General Staff became increasingly concerned about a possible ground invasion. You'll see this in the collegium of 4 February 1999, which is Exhibit P932 at pages 10 and 11. On 18 February 1999, General Antic reported that the number of NATO forces in Macedonia will be raised to 8.000 at the end of February. General Ojdanic indicated that he had taken the position to call-up and deploy troops to areas near the border with Kosovo so that they can be deployed there rapidly. It was clear that this build-up of troops was to defend against a possible NATO invasion and not to expel the Albanian population. When explaining why he had decided to call-up more troops, General Ojdanic expressly said on this occasion: "We must defend the country if we are attacked. Politics and diplomacy will do everything to resolve this by peaceful means if possible." That's at page 18 of Exhibit P937. On 11 March 1999, General Ojdanic said at the collegium that the OSCE knew full well why the Yugoslavian army had increased and deployed more troops. He said, and I summarize here: NATO is getting 9.500 people on board down there, we don't know whether they will use them to invade, but we can't sit here and be unprepared. That's at pages 21 and 22 of Exhibit P935. On 18 March 1999, at the collegium, General Ojdanic again stated that the army had increased its forces in and around Kosovo because of the NATO build-up of troops in Macedonia. That's at page 7, Exhibit P938. Therefore, it's clear from these discussions over the course of February and March 1999, that the build-up of troops of the Yugoslav forces had nothing to do with any plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo. In fact, at the collegium on 4 March 1999, it was reported that the KLA was trying to provoke incidents of excessive use of force or a humanitarian crisis so as to generate international intervention, and that the possibility of the KLA provoking massive movements of refugees in order to create again a humanitarian -- a humanitarian catastrophe situation could not be excluded. General Dimitrijevic specifically reported intelligence that very organised activities of the KLA were moving civilians from individual villages to bring the humanitarian crisis to the fore again and provoke -- provoke a reaction from the international community. You'll find that on pages 4 through 9 of Exhibit P933. Therefore, not only is there not a single mention of a plan by the Yugoslav Army to expel Albanians from Kosovo, but it's clear that the General Staff believed that it was the KLA who wanted the population to move. Had a plan to expel Albanians been in existence to the knowledge of the General Staff, it is inconceivable that it not -- it would not have at least been alluded to in the collegiums. The discussion -- the discussion at the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request that the speaker slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. I've been -- I've been requested to slow down. I apologise to the interpreters, and I assure you my colleague, Mr. Visnjic, has been very keenly after me. The -- the discussion at the collegium of 9 April 1999 is particularly important to understand what General Ojdanic knew about the movement of the population from Kosovo. It's clear that he believed that it was the KLA, not the Serb forces, who were causing the movement of people from Kosovo. General Krga, in charge of the intelligence administration, described the movement as "the planned withdrawal of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army and Siptar people from Kosovo which has realistically created a difficult humanitarian situation." That's at page 5 of the collegium, which is Exhibit P929. General Gajic, who was the head of security administration, said at the same collegium that: "After crushing the terrorist forces in Kosovo, some of them managed, probably in a planned way, to withdraw to Albania, Macedonia, and a few to Montenegro." He predicts that the terrorists will force Albanian and non-Albanian citizens to move out of Kosovo. He goes on to say that: "The enemy will conduct planned activity to push out Siptars in order to accuse the army and the state of ethnic cleansing and genocide, thereby creating more favourable conditions for operations by NATO against our forces." That's at pages 8 through 11 of Exhibit P929. On that same day, April 9, 1999, General Ojdanic issued a directive which indicated that the army expected infiltration by KLA on the pretext of securing the return of the refugees; that reception of refugees on the state border should be organised; that the army should offer assistance to other organs of government for the further care of the refugees; that infiltration of the returning refugees by the KLA should be prevented; and that the enemy should be treated in accord with international humanitarian law. That's Exhibit P1481. It's therefore clear that as of 9 April 1999 at the level of the staff of the Supreme Command, the displacement of the refugees was believed to have been a KLA tactic to stimulate international support; that it was seen as against the interests of the army; and that the return of the refugees was not only contemplated but was to be facilitated. This is hardly consistent with a joint criminal enterprise to deport Kosovo-Albanians. In fact, the Prosecution witness, General Vasiljevic, testified that he was certain there was no plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo. He said that if such a plan existed, it would have had to have been discussed at the daily meetings of the Supreme Command Staff attended by a representative of the security organs and no such discussion, in fact, took place. You'll find his testimony in the transcript of 22 January 2007 at page 8840. There is simply no evidence from which any -- from any witness or document that General Ojdanic ever agreed to, had knowledge of, or participated in any enterprise or operation which had as its objective the expulsion of Albanians from Kosovo. This fact alone requires a finding that the Prosecution has not proven its case against General Ojdanic for individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. In short, the Prosecution's case against General Ojdanic for individual criminal liability comes down to this: Because the expulsion of Albanians was widespread all across Kosovo, it must have been the result of a plan, a joint criminal enterprise. However, taking the Prosecution's evidence at its highest, giving them the benefit of all doubt, there is simply no evidence that expulsions were planned or ordered at the level of the General Staff. The Prosecution cannot substitute inference for evidence, particularly where the involvement of the General Staff is not the only reasonable inference available from the evidence. Other reasonable inferences in support of the Prosecutor's theory, such as the bad behaviour of individual soldiers or units or coordination by other bodies on the ground in Kosovo, may be more readily drawn from the evidence heard by the Trial Chamber. As the Appeals Chamber has recently said in the Galic appeals judgement, "Findings at trial based on circumstantial evidence must be the only reasonable conclusions available from that evidence. If there is another conclusion which is also reasonably open from the circumstantial evidence and which is consistent with the innocence of the accused, he must be acquitted." Putting aside the substantial questions of whether a joint criminal enterprise or even a plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo ever existed, one thing is abundantly clear. There is no evidence - I repeat - no evidence upon which this Trial Chamber could conclude that General Ojdanic participated in such an enterprise or plan. For that reason, he must acquitted on charges of individual criminal liability under Article 7(1) on each count of the indictment. I'd like now to turn to the events in Kosovo beginning on 24 March 1999 and the question of General Ojdanic's superior responsibility under Article 7(3): The failure to prevent or punish crimes submitted -- committed by his subordinates. The Appeals Chamber has held that to hold a commander responsible for the crimes of his subordinates, it must be established beyond reasonable doubt: First, there existed a superior/subordinate relationship between the superior and the perpetrator of the crime; second, the superior knew or had reason to know that the criminal act was about to be or had been committed; and three, the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal act or to punish the perpetrator thereof. I take that from the Kordic Appeals Chamber judgement 17th December 2004 at paragraph 827. For the purposes of this agreement, let's assume that the Prosecution has introduced evidence from which the Trial Chamber could find that some of the crimes alleged in the indictment were committed in Kosovo by members of the Yugoslavian Army. I don't know to what extent, if any, my colleagues will address the crime-based evidence in this case, but for purposes of assessing General Ojdanic's criminal responsibility in this motion, let's assume that the first element has been established; that at least some of the crimes charged in the indictment were committed in Kosovo by persons who were subordinate to General Ojdanic. And by "subordinates," I'm using the word in the most general sense, since in fact there were at least five degrees of separation between General Ojdanic in Belgrade and any soldiers who may have committed crimes in Kosovo. The soldiers were subordinate to the company commander, the battalion commander, the brigade commander, the corps commander, the 3rd Army commander, and finally to General Ojdanic as Chief of Staff. It may well be that despite the fact that some perpetrators of the crimes were soldiers in the army and, therefore, technically subordinate to General Ojdanic, he did not have the requisite "effective control" over them, as required by relevant case law to satisfy the first element of Article 7(3). But again, we're in a 98 bis motion, so let's assume for purposes of this 98 bis motion that at least some of the crimes in the indictment were committed by persons who were subordinates of General Ojdanic and over whom he exercised effective control. Let's assume that arguendo. So let's turn then to the second requirement, and that is the issue of knowledge. What is the evidence that General Ojdanic knew or had reason to know that any of the specific crimes charged in the indictment "was about to be or had been committed"? And the answer, I respectfully suggest, is: None. You heard from General Vasiljevic that it was the regular practice for brigades to submit daily combat reports to the Pristina Corps command. The corps command condensed the information into a single report, which was forwarded to the 3rd Army. The 3rd Army would condense the reports from the corps and send it on to the Supreme Command Staff. You'll find that testimony in the transcript of 18 January 2007 at page 8661. The daily combat reports of the Pristina Corps were also copied to the staff of the Supreme Command in Belgrade. I submit to you that there is no evidence that any of the crimes charged in the indictment were included in any of the daily reports received by General Ojdanic or the Supreme Command Staff, nor is there any testimony from anyone that they had brought any of the specify crimes listed in the indictment to General Ojdanic's attention. There is evidence in these reports that, in general, crimes were being committed in Kosovo, and they were being addressed by the military justice system. Pristina Corps daily combat reports, beginning on 3 April 1998 [sic], reported that during the preceding days, 32 criminal reports were submitted against the perpetrators for crimes: eight for murder; one for abuse; three for attempted murder; two for taking vehicles; six for theft; and 12 for absence without official leave. That's Exhibit 5D84. Other Pristina Corps daily combat reports containing similar information, which are in evidence, include the report of 4 April 1999, which is Exhibit P2617; the report of 13 April 1999, which is Exhibit P2004; the report of 25 April 1999, which is Exhibit 2016; 9 May 1999, Exhibit P2006; 12 May 1999, Exhibit P2007. We also have some of the daily reports of the 3rd Army to the staff of the Supreme Command in evidence. For example, the report of 20 April 1999, which is Exhibit P1945, informed the General Staff that: "Individual cases of violation of order and discipline had been registered and were successfully dealt with. Units of the military police carrying out -- are carrying out -- successfully carrying out tasks that fall within their competence." You'll find that on page 4.
