In the 3rd Army daily report of 27 April 1999, it was indicated that military prosecutors are processing 89 criminal reports and had issued 11 indictments. First-instance courts had received 38 requests for investigation and 10 indictments. That's on page 2 of Exhibit P2005. Two days later, on 29 April 1999, it was reported that military prosecutors had received 116 criminal reports and first-instance courts had received 15 indictments. That's from page 2 of Exhibit P2017. Similar reports can be found in the 3rd Army reports of 20 May 1999, which is Exhibit P2008 at page 4. In a Pristina Corps daily report of 9 May 1999, it was reported that: "The population is treated correctly and humanely." An example was given of how soldiers had found a group of Albanian refugees in the woods and taken them to a nearby school where they were supplied with heating, oil, and food. You'll find that at page 4 of Exhibit P2006. And parenthetically may I note here the testimony of Shaun Byrnes, who was quite clear in saying that in his opinion the VJ, both before and during the conflict, acted honourably and correctly. So a review of these reports indicates that the staff of the Supreme Command was being informed in general of the commission of some crimes in Kosovo and was being consistently assured that these crimes were being adequately addressed by the military justice organs. The evidence also shows that, during this period, General Ojdanic took measures to prevent crimes in Kosovo. On 2 April 1999, he issued an order to treat prisoners humanely and to undertake prosecution against any army member who fails to adhere to international humanitarian law, and that the combat reports be upgraded to include instances of failure to obey humanitarian laws. That's at Exhibit 3D480. On the 7th of April, General Ojdanic issued an order that required full screening of volunteers. He directed that his subordinates pay special attention to the results of the psychiatric examination he had required for all volunteers to establish the suitability of volunteers from a security point of view, to prohibit the grouping of volunteers in one unit, to inform each volunteer that the illegal behave -- that illegal behaviour will not be tolerated and will be punished and to strictly prohibit paramilitaries. You'll find that order as Exhibit P1479. General Ojdanic issued another order on 14 April 1999, which directed that a sufficient number of security organs, military police, and psychologists must be engaged at reception centres for volunteers, emphasised the volunteers must undergo psychological screening and training, insisted that there be training on the consequences of unlawful behaviour, and that it be clearly stated that any such conduct will prosecuted. General Ojdanic once again forbid volunteers to be grouped into separate units. That's all in Exhibit 3D481. And finally, on this aspect of the case I call to the Trial Chamber's attention a communication dated 20 April 1999 from the Supreme Command Staff, that's Prosecution Exhibit 1943. This communication is critical of the 1st Army for sending volunteers in its area for service in the 3rd Army, where of course the war was going on, including the fact that a number of the volunteers had a prior criminal record and also citing paramilitary volunteers who were unfit for military service. And this document says specifically several days -- and I'm reading from P1943: "Several days after receiving the volunteers, 20 of them were returned from the Pristina Corps and seven of them were detained for outlawry, murder, rape, refusing to obey orders, and desertion." The report goes on to say: "A number of volunteers, around 50 per cent subsequently gave up their deployment and engagement in the VJ Yugoslav Army RJ war units, reserve units stating that they were not ready to obey the orders unreservedly." And finally report says: "Based on the above stated take measures in order to eliminate the problems and oversights that were noted -- and to entirely secure execution of the order issued by the Chief of the Supreme Command Staff dated 14 April 1999." And that was the prior order of General Ojdanic outlining more stringent screening and entreatment of volunteers and paramilitaries. General Ojdanic's insistence that international humanitarian law be obeyed by the soldiers under his command continued throughout the period of the war. On 16 April 1999, he issued a warning labelled "very urgent" that he transmitted to all army units in Kosovo, reiterating that international law must be observed and that all organs must prevent and report criminal acts. "During combat so far," reading from the report -- reading from General Ojdanic's transmission. "During combat so far, according to some information, there have been isolated cases of conduct when the provisions of the instructions and guide-lines on conduct and the provisions of the international law of war were not fully complied with. Some commands and units do not pay due attention to combatting isolated cases of looting and crimes. Commands and professional organs shall undertake effective measures to prevent all forms of criminal acts. Inform all members of the VJ about the damaging consequences of all forms of criminal activity to the population and morale of the army." That's Exhibit 3D482. And then on April 25th, 1999, General Vasiljevic was called out of retirement and given the task of investigating and reporting to the staff of the Supreme Command about crimes committed in Kosovo. On 26 April 1999, General Ojdanic issued another order that provided that paramilitaries are to be disarmed and legal measures taken against them that violators of international law are to be apprehended, prosecuted, and the superior command levels informed, that the Geneva Conventions and rules of law are to be consistently and rigorously obeyed, and that superior officers are to be held responsible for this. You'll find this order in Exhibit P1902. On 10 May 1999, General Ojdanic issued yet another order emphasising that commanders were obligated to take all necessary steps to prevent violations of international humanitarian law and warning them that they'll be held personally responsible if they don't. You'll find this as Exhibit 3D483. Also in evidence is a report of 7 May 1999, which is Exhibit P1917. In that report, the staff of the Supreme Command was informed that after initial difficulties, the organs of the military justice system are now working according to wartime conditions, and that military prosecutors and military courts are being reinforced. Another report on the work of military judicial organs in wartime was prepared on 12 May 1999. The report noted that military judicial operations had been put in operation as soon as a state of war was proclaimed, but that the large number of criminal reports required replenishment of these organs with professional and experienced personnel. The report notes that the initial deficiencies were relatively quickly eliminated. The report further noted that the military judicial organs at the command of the Pristina Corps had encountered very complex criminal cases concerning serious crimes, and that it was necessary that legally valid proofs be included in the criminal reports. It concluded with recommendations for improving the efficiency of the military judicial organs. You'll find this report at Exhibit P1918. Meanwhile, as you've heard from the testimony of General Vasiljevic, on 13 May 1999, there was a modest celebration of the day of the establishment of the security services. The representatives of the security department were received by General Ojdanic. On that occasion, General Geza acquainted General Ojdanic with the information that General Vasiljevic had learned from his mission to Kosovo. General Vasiljevic testified that General Ojdanic was very taken aback by what he was told. How while the officers were still there, he called President Milosevic and informed him that he had just received information from security organs that there was serious problems with crimes being committed in Kosovo. General Vasiljevic further testified that a meeting was scheduled for the 17th of May with President Milosevic. General Ojdanic then called General Pavkovic and summoned him to Belgrade to report directly to General Ojdanic what was going on. According to General Vasiljevic, General Ojdanic explicitly stressed that nothing should be concealed or cover -- or covered up, and that everything that had happened be put forward, and that it has to be seen whether any measures and what measures had been taken to deal with such developments. You'll find that testimony from General -- from General Vasiljevic in the transcript 19 January 2007, at pages 8748 and 8749. General Vasiljevic also told you of the meeting held at the Supreme Command on 16 May 1999 prior to the meeting with President Milosevic. At this meeting, General Pavkovic spoke about crimes that were allegedly committed. General Vasiljevic testified that from the reaction of General Ojdanic at this meeting and the meeting of May 13, he concluded that General Ojdanic had not been informed of the extent of the crimes that had been committed in Kosovo. You'll find that testimony in the transcript of 19 January 2007, at pages 8755 and 8768. These crimes were discussed in full during the meeting on 17 May 1999 with President Milosevic and representatives of the Ministry of Interior and state security. According to General Vasiljevic, General Ojdanic and Pavkovic proposed an independent state commission to investigate war crimes in Kosovo. You'll find that testimony in the transcript of 22 January 2007, at page 8783. Although this commission was never established, General Ojdanic continued to make his own efforts to see that crimes in Kosovo were prevented and punished. According to General Vasiljevic on 26 May 1999, orders were issued to improve the functioning of the military courts. General Ojdanic then convened a meeting on 28 May 1999 with the heads of the military judicial organs and General Farkas, in which he informed them that their bodies were required to act more vigorously. You'll find that testimony in the transcript of 22 January 2007, at page 8878. And you can see from the report of 30 May 1999, which is Exhibit P1899, that daily reports of the functioning of the military courts began to be compiled and provided to the Supreme Command Staff. General Vasiljevic also testified that after the meeting of 17 May, General Ojdanic sent him and General Geza to Kosovo to gather more detailed information about what was going on concerning crimes, looting, and the other problems that were reported at the meeting. General Vasiljevic learned during his investigation that there had been a decision by the army command in Pristina not to report the commission of some crimes, but General Vasiljevic went on to say that the 3rd Army had investigated and processed these cases, and therefore they thought it unnecessary to further report these particular cases up the chain of command. You'll find that in the transcript of 19 January 2007, at pages 8647, 8651. You also heard testimony from Mr. Djordjevic about the pressure put on the military judicial organs, the lack of credibility of the testimony of this disgruntled individual is a matter which I recognise is not properly before you at this stage of the proceedings in deciding on a motion for judgement of acquittal. But even if his testimony is taken at face value, which we must do in a 98 bis hearing, even if it's taken at face value, it provides no facts to believe that General Ojdanic was involved in or aware of any efforts to extricate certain individual from prosecution -- certain individuals from prosecution for crimes they committed on the ground in Kosovo. You can see that on the 8th of June, as the extent of these crimes began to come to light at the level of the Supreme Command, a briefing was held by the Supreme Command Staff. According to the notes of this briefing, which is Exhibit 3D493, General Geza reported that a full analysis had been made of the problems involving humanitarian crime. He said that most of the atrocities and serious crimes from looting to rapes had been documented and were now before military court organs. He said that around 95 per cent of the perpetrators had been arrested or under investigation. At this meeting, General Ojdanic issued a document ordering that military judicial organs should prioritise their prosecution of crimes, and that violations of international law must be the first priority. You'll find that document at Exhibit 3D487. Therefore, the evidence in this case shows that General Ojdanic had no knowledge of the specific crimes alleged in the indictment, and therefore no ability or duty to prevent or punish them. The evidence also shows that he was affirmatively informed that the movement of the population was the result of KLA action, not that of the army. And the evidence showed that when he was informed in a general way of violations of international humanitarian law being committed by members of the army in Kosovo, he took swift and repeated steps to investigate, prevent, and punish those crimes. A review of the jurisprudence that sets out the standards of a top commander, such as General Ojdanic, shows that his actions were appropriate and proper. Starting with the high command case at Nuremberg after World War II when assessing the liability of the defendant Vonleeb, the Tribunal noted that a Chief of Staff is not automatically criminally responsible for the criminal acts of soldiers under his command. The Tribunal said that a high commander "has the right to assume that details entrusted to responsible subordinates will be legally executed." It must be proven that there was some individual breach of his responsibilities by that commander. You'll find that language in volume 12 of the Law Reports of Trials of War Criminals at page 76. At the trials held in Tokyo after World War II, the Tribunal also recognised the reality faced by top commanders. The court said: "In the multitude of duties and tasked involved in modern government, there is of necessity an elaborate system of subdivision and delegation of duties." The court held that: "The responsibility of senior commanders is twofold. First they must establish a system that secures proper treatment, in that case of prisoners of war; and second, they must take steps to secure the system's continued and efficient working." It was also held that: "A senior commander cannot be expected to be intimately familiar with all the day-to-day operations of his subordinate units, rather, it is his responsibility to establish systems that will ensure law of war compliance and then provide command oversight of those systems." You can find this jurisprudence in the Pritchard edition of the proceedings of the Tokyo major war crimes at pages 443 through 448. This concept was codified some 50 years later in the Statute of the International Criminal Court, which explicitly provides in Article 28 for a commander's duty to take all necessary and reasonable measures within his or her power to prevent or repress the commission of crimes or to submit the matter to the competent authorities for investigation and prosecution. At this Tribunal, four Trial Chambers have endorsed the view that the question whether all necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of crimes or to punish the perpetrators have been taken must be considered in light of the accused's material powers at that time. Factors relevant to the Chamber's assessment include whether specific orders prohibiting or stopping the criminal activities were issued; what measures to secure the implementation of these orders were taken; what other measures were taken to secure that the unlawful acts were interrupted; and whether these measures were reasonably sufficient in the specific circumstances. And after the commission of the crime, what steps were taken to secure an adequate investigation and to bring the perpetrators to justice. You'll find that in the judgement in the Strugar case at paragraph 378; the Halilovic case, at paragraph 74; the Limaj case at paragraph 528; and the Hadzihasanovic judgement, at paragraphs 147 and 1043 to 1067. General Hadzihasanovic was held not -- was held not responsible for failing to punish Bosnian army subordinate soldiers who killed unarmed prisoners because he turned the matter over to the judicial system. The accused was informed that executions may have occurred, but concluded that the deaths were combat related. Pursuant to local procedure, the military police then referred the matter to the military court. Evidence established that the court did not punish the perpetrators; however, since the accused turned the matter over to the appropriate authority without reason to suspect a crime was committed, he was held not to have failed to take reasonable measures. And again that's in paragraphs 1043 to 1063 of the Hadzihasanovic judgement. In the Blaskic case, the accused was held not responsible by the Appeals Court for failing to punish subordinate crimes because he had submitted the case to competent authorities. Despite never receiving a satisfactory report regarding the alleged incident, the Court found that the accused's obligation, by virtue of the duties of his position, was to call for an investigation. By doing so, the accused had fulfilled his duty, despite the fact the investigators allowed the crime to go unpunished. You'll find that at paragraphs 412 through 422 of the Blaskic appeals judgement. From the evidence produced by the Prosecution in this case, you can see that as Chief of Staff in Belgrade, General Ojdanic had no specific information about the crimes alleged in the indictment. Given the attitude and actions he displayed consistently throughout the war, it is clear that if he had had such information, he would have referred the matters to the competent military judicial authorities and insisted that the perpetrators of these crimes be prosecuted. It is also clear that during the course of the war, General Ojdanic received general information that crimes were being committed by members of the army, but at the same time he was receiving consistent information that these crimes were being addressed by the military justice authorities, who were the competent authorities to handle such matters. When he first began receiving information of more extensive problems with crimes in Kosovo, General Ojdanic took swift and decisive action. He ordered an investigation, insisted on receiving reports on the situation from his subordinates, immediately brought the matter to the attention of his own superior President Milosevic, and issued a series of directives and orders, insisting on obedience to international humanitarian law, threatening superiors with personal consequences for breaches by their subordinates, and strengthening the military justice system. It is our respectful submission that there is no evidence from which the Trial Chamber could find that General Ojdanic failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent and punish crimes committed in Kosovo. The Prosecution's own case is replete with frequent and repeated efforts by General Ojdanic to meet and exceed his obligation as a commander to prevent and punish such crimes. These efforts are all the more extraordinary when one considers the circumstances under which General Ojdanic was operating, facing a daily barrage of bombs dropping all over the territory of Serbia by the combined forces of the greatest superpowers in the world. The philosopher and statesman Edmund Burke said: "All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing." The Prosecution's case in this courtroom has indeed shown that evil deeds were committed in Kosovo against Albanians, just as its case in another courtroom is showing that evil deeds were committed in Kosovo against Serbs. But the Prosecution's own evidence has shown that General Ojdanic was not one of those who did evil, and he was not one of those who did nothing; rather, as you heard from General Loncar, General Perisic [sic], and General Vasiljevic, General Ojdanic was a good man, a good soldier, and a good commander who acted professionally and without ethnic hatred or discrimination. No witness in this entire trial has said a bad word about him. The documentary evidence in the Prosecution's own case is replete with his tireless efforts to do the right thing. There is simply no evidence upon which this Trial Chamber could find him guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. We're not here to ask you to make fine distinctions or to rely on procedural niceties; the truth is that General Ojdanic is innocent. He's here because Prosecutor Louise Arbour made a political decision to indict the top officials of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as the bombing dragged on in May 1999, as just another weapon in NATO's arsenal. There was no evidence of General Ojdanic's criminal responsibility then, and there is no evidence of it now. He does not belong here. We ask you to grant General Ojdanic's motion for judgement of acquittal and put an end now, please, to this prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Ackerman -- I'm sorry. I gather -- just one moment, Mr. Ackerman. Judge Chowhan has a question for Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Somewhere in the middle of your learned arguments, you mentioned about the troops being sent to protect the Serbs, VJ troops were being sent. Keeping this in mind, I take it to be a national organisation, and the way you put it and the way I understood it appeared as if a national organisation was only concerned about some of the ethnic groups and not all. And nowhere it was said that the VJ sent troops or men or materiel for any other ethnic group in that way in which you -- which you put it for the troops having gone for protection of one of the ethnic groups. Being a national army it -- what impression was it giving or should it not have given an impression that it belongs to everybody in that sense of the term and the overall tumultuous situation should have been brought to an end not because A was there, B was there, C was there, but it was a national duty for a national organisation to see that it goes down and help anybody without any such feelings as I gathered from this. I mean, this is what you -- if you wish to, rather, explain, this may be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful for you taking this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, you said about the middle of my arguments. I'm assuming you're referring to what I had to say about Podujevo, about the presence in Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the reason I was focusing rather heavily on the Serb population was that the overwhelming majority of the folks there, you know, many of the folks there were Albanian, but the Serbs were leaving the place in droves. And so that was the concern. The concern was to protect these Serbian civilians who were, again, requesting protection from the army. It's not that the army was indifferent to Albanian civilians, but since -- because there was a strong KLA presence there, I think the Albanians certainly were comfortable, you know, in an area where there was a strong KLA presence. And there is nothing to indicate that any of the General Staff certainly had any negative feelings about Albanians or would not have responded, for example, had Albanian citizens protested, because there were very many Albanian citizens who were treated very poorly and very shabbily by the KLA. And in that kind of a situation I would find it really incredible that the Serb forces would not have given assistance under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But there was no such illustration referred to by your good self in your learned discourse to have actually supported this view which you are now holding. Any such occasion where it may have happened for any other ethnic group? I mean, some sort of indication that I thought -- if that was possible. I'm grateful again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right. Well, there were all sorts of reports during the trial by the Kosovo Verification Mission of improper treatment of Albanians by the KLA, murders, kidnappings of those thought to be collaborationists. And I think the evidence is quite clear that in that kind of a situation the MUP responded to that. They didn't ignore it, they investigated it and treated it very, very seriously. There were a number of instances, Your Honour, which showed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I should say thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I assume we'll break at 5.30. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm happy to have this opportunity to address you on behalf of General Pavkovic. As you've no doubt noticed, my colleagues have covered a lot of ground that would be appropriate for me to cover when I'm speaking to you only by myself. So I'm not going to go through the process of repeating a number of the things that my colleagues have already expressed to you, many of those things being their analyses of the law which primarily I'm in totally in agreement with. My intention, as I begin, is to adopt at least in some measure the recommendations of Your Honour Judge Bonomy several weeks ago when you said, The 98 bis process is one where really all the Defence has to do is stand up and say the case was not proven, and then it's up to the Prosecutor to -- to make a showing. Now, that paragraph was written by me about five or six weeks ago, and since then a number of pages have -- have come into this process. I still think I can complete my remarks in maybe about an hour, and that's what I'll try to do. I'm not going to go into huge detail about the evidence you've heard in this case. I've watched you pay attention. I've watched you make notes. I don't have to tell you what the various witnesses have said, although there's been a huge amount of material to try to -- to get our hands around. And I'll try to help just a little bit with that. Over a hundred years ago, General William Tecumseh Sherman, a civil war confederate general in the United States said: "War is hell." And it is. Perhaps more so now than then. Almost every day, we hear of the hell of war. We hear about Iraq; we hear about Afghanistan; we hear about Somalia; and Darfur; and Sri Lanka; where things are in many ways similar to what happened in the Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 are going on in front of us today. Although war is hell, it's legal. Was is not illegal. Modern war is very different from the Napoleonic wars that many of us learned about in grade school and high school. They're not wars fought on the battle-fields and the countryside, they're wars that are fought among the civilian population in the villages and in the cities. Most often they're wars these days brought on by insurgencies or terrorists seeking to overthrow a government and take control of a state, rather than war as between two states over territory. This kind of modern warfare certainly describes what we've learned about in Kosovo. And in these kinds of wars, civilians die in numbers that I think we all believe are unacceptable, and that we would change if there was any way we could. Every day we hear about such things. Just yesterday, the BBC reported about an incident in Afghanistan where NATO was attacking a Taleban group, who as usual were mingled among the civilian population, resulting perhaps in the death of as many as 30 civilians. There was no intention on the part of NATO to kill those civilians, but there was an intention to deal with a very difficult situation that is facing those forces in Afghanistan at this time. Modern wars also produce crowds of refugees. That's not the goal of these wars, but it's an inevitable byproduct of them. When a war is fought among the citizenry with modern weapons, what happens is intense fear; intense fear causes persons to flee. Just look at the huge numbers of refugees who have fled the country of Iraq since it was invaded nearly five years ago. Modern military leaders have studied in their schools these modern wars as they were coming up through the ranks in their various military organisations. They learned that a feature of such wars is this mass exodus of civilians from war zones. People run from bombs and guns. I would. You would. Anybody would. Nobody needs to tell us to get out of harm's way. So the mere reality of refugees does not automatically suggest that someone forced them to leave their homes by committing some kind of a war crime. Responsible people make efforts to save themselves, and that's what refugees mostly are doing around this world today. So when we ask, Was it NATO or the KLA or the Serbs or some other factor that forced the people of Kosovo to flee, we could be ignoring the fact that war is hell, and it frightens people, and they run from it. The real answer of why people leave their homes in war is because they're afraid. They're seeking safety. They're looking for a place where bombs are not falling and guns are not firing. We can't expect what happened in Kosovo to be one of these old-fashioned, clean Napoleonic countryside wars. It was modern war, and it was war instigated by terrorists. Every modern war also carries with it atrocities of one form or another. The men who fight these wars are traditionally very young. In some cases, we've seen in Africa even children. It's easy to get young people to fight; that's why our soldiers are young people. They have little sense of their own mortality. They tend to see themselves as bullet-proof, so they'll enter the foray and charge up the hill when asked to do so. And unfortunately, some of them commit war crimes. They do things they know they're not supposed to do. And no matter the effort made by commanders to prevent the rapes and the murders and the beatings and the tortures, they happen in wars. They happen with British and American soldiers in Iraq and Afghanistan; they happen wherever we see a war going on. Because we're human and because we care, we really, when we hear about these matters, want to believe there must be someone who's responsible for this that we can blame and punish. There must be somebody we can find that we can put the onus on for what these youths do when they're handed guns and told to go fight. There must be some evil person who has orchestrated this misbehaviour by these young people. So we begin to look at leaders and try to find some justification for the behaviour of our children. We don't want to believe that our children could do the things we hear about, and so we do things like we're doing here. But what we also know if we look at the major cities of this world, largely in American, Britain, crimes are committed by youth on the streets of those cities. Children with guns, youth committing crimes, youth committing rapes, youth committing murders. They do it every day in the cities of my country. And there, they're not under the direction of anybody, they're just kids committing crimes. That's what they do. Why are we surprised then when they do the same thing in a war zone, when we've made it even easier for them by handing them a gun and lots of ammunition and cutting them loose? It's so easy for them to step over a line. We need to acknowledge that leaders cannot prevent this type of activity. Look at every war that you've ever seen in your lifetime, and no leader has yet been able to prevent this kind of activity. Efforts are made, no doubt, and efforts have been made by the leaders in this case, as Mr. Sepenuk has so thoroughly covered for you. But those efforts are not always successful. In fact, they're not ever successful. I'm sure that the -- the commanders in the Yugoslav Army and the orders they issued are no less than the commanders in the British Army and the American Army issued as they went into Iraq to begin that adventure there. Kosovo is not a World War II story. It was not some rogue state trying to brutally conquer territory. It was a people seeking to preserve a country against attack by well-armed and well-financed terrorists who were seeking to overthrow the government and take control of that part of that state. I want to talk for a moment about joint criminal enterprise because that's a significant issue in this case. I assume most of you would have had an opportunity to take a look at the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Brdjanin case where joint criminal enterprise was discussed at some length. And unusually, the Appeals Chamber relied pretty heavily on some work that our own Judge Bonomy had done earlier regarding joint criminal enterprise. Judge Bonomy had analysed a couple of World War II vintage cases, and those analyses were found to be compelling and helpful by the Appeals Chamber. The first of those, the Justice case. The Justice case involved an accused by the name of Lautz. He was the chief public prosecutor of the people's court, and he issued indictments against Poles, charging them with high treason for leaving their places of work and attempting to escape German -- Germany by crossing into Switzerland. He was following a clear plan of racial discrimination. The Poles that he indicted were all of them sentenced to death and executed. To an extent, he defended on the basis that he didn't execute any of those people. All he did was issue an indictment. But the fact that he took that step made him guilty for the death of those people. But what you see there and what Judge Bonomy saw there was a link and an action by Lautz ultimately resulting in the death of the people that he directly brought indictments against. Rothaug was also convicted for his role in convicting and sentencing to death three Poles and a Jew in conformity with this discriminatory policy of persecution, torture and extermination of the Jewish and Polish races. The defence that the executioners were separate from Rothaug and Lautz was not a defence that was allowed to carry any water. Their responsibility was based on actions performed by them. They ordered prosecutions and executions in furtherance of this plan. You will find no orders by General Pavkovic, in this case, ordering any kind of comparable activity or ordering the commission of any kind of an offence. They also talked about what Judge Bonomy wrote with regard to the Rusha case, Hofmann and Hildebrandt. In response to contentions by the accused, quoting Judge Bonomy, that they did not themselves physically perpetrate any crimes, the Tribunal held that it is no defence for a defendant to insist, for instance, that he never evacuated populations when orders exist signed by him in which he directed that the evacuation should take place. While in such a case the defendant might not have actually carried out the physical evacuation in the sense that he did not personally evacuate the population, he nevertheless is responsible for the action. And his participation by instigating the action is more pronounced than that of those who actually performed the deed." Again, in this case, you'll find no comparable order by General Pavkovic. The Brdjanin case discussed this question of the necessity of the Prosecution to prove links between the individual that's charged and the perpetrators who commit the crimes. At paragraph 412, the Appeals Chamber wrote: "As the Prosecution recognises for it to be possible to hold an accused responsible for the criminal conduct of another person, there must be a link between the accused and the crime as legal basis for the imputation of criminal liability." Paragraph 418: "The Appeals Chamber understands that the Trial Chamber's disputed finding was reached out of a concern that it is inappropriate to impose liability on an accused where the link, between him or her and those who physically perpetrated the crimes for which he or she is charged, is too tenuous. The Appeals Chamber shares this concern." Judge Van Den Wyngaert, in a separate declaration in the Brdjanin case, I think sheds significant light on these issues when she wrote at paragraph 4: "The judgement of the Appeals Chamber clearly shows that JCE is not an open-ended formula that allows convictions based on guilt by association. I am in full agreement with the conclusions of the judgement on the doctrine of joint criminal enterprise, where these limits are strictly drawn, based on a careful analysis of customary international law and of the Tribunal's own case law. The link between the accused and the criminal conduct of the principal perpetrator does not follow from the perpetrator's membership of the JCE but from the actual contribution of the accused to the JCE which must be significant." It's not enough, Your Honours, for the Prosecution to show you that crimes were committed. There is no modern war that doesn't involve the commission of crimes. There must be a link between the accused and the perpetrator who committed the crime, as described above, even in a JCE situation. This case is highly unique among the kinds of cases that I was discussing as I started my remarks. And I think maybe, Your Honour, I should go into this after we come back from our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We'll break now and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I talked about other wars that we're familiar with. World War II lasted for six years. What's going on in Iraq has been going on now for, like, five years. If you look at Kosovo, the crime base for Kosovo covers a period of about five weeks. The whole conflict was 78 days from March 24th until the Serb forces were -- left Kosovo. But the crime base is over a period of about five weeks. That's a very, very short time for high-level commanders to learn about events occurring, to react to those events, to take prevention and punishment measures. The other thing that must be clearly kept in mind was when that conflict ended and the Serb forces left Kosovo, the opportunity to investigate what went on in some of the villages was not there any longer. No more investigation could be done. Serb forces were not allowed into Kosovo after that. For the most part, even though we know crimes were committed, murders were committed in those villages, we don't know who committed those crimes. The Prosecution has spent years trying to find out who committed the crimes, largely without success, but argues that a general like Pavkovic so far removed from the action should have known about those crimes and who committed them almost instantly. That defies all logic. After many years of investigation, eight years, what the Prosecutor's been able to tell us in most cases is the colour of the uniforms worn by the perpetrators and nothing more. We need to understand that people who commit war crimes don't go around bragging about their crimes and even their immediate superiors, the company commanders, are not all that anxious to report that people under their command committed crimes for fear of what might happen to them. We know that crimes notoriously are covered up by their perpetrators whether they're committed in war or on the streets of the cities of the world. You must ask when did General Pavkovic learn of the crimes that make up the crime base in this case? You're not going to find that out from the evidence you've heard. Perhaps he only learned it only when he read the indictment. The Prosecution must prove that he had knowledge of these crimes, and that he failed to prevent and punish them. We must ask what he failed to do. Where in the evidence is there something that General Pavkovic should have done that he failed to do? You have before you an indictment charging my client, General Pavkovic, with the commission in various indirect ways of crimes from the year 1999. You've heard evidence of criminal activity in 1999 from residents of villages in Kosovo, some credible, some not so credible, but none of them implicate General Pavkovic in any way. What you've mostly heard, however, strangely, has been about matters that occurred in 1998. Witness after witness after witness could only testify about 1998. Virtually all of the international witnesses you've heard could only give evidence about 1998. If the OTP has a case against anyone for 1998 events, they have no indictment for 1998 events. They do have an indictment for 1999, but they have no case. One of the things that kept cropping up - and I suggest it was virtually a red herring in this case - was that whole thread of evidence trying to establish that General Pavkovic was operating outside the chain of command in 1998. First of all, it's 1998. Whether he was operating outside the chain of command in 1998 seems to me to have little effect on the indictment charges for what happened in 1999. It should be clear to you that the Prosecution's allegations in this regard have failed. The evidence is, at best, speculative and, at worst, simply false. It appears that General Perisic may have started making a case for his own absolution very early on by making false allegations against others, maybe not. I can't offer any more proof of that than the Prosecution has offered you that General Pavkovic was operating outside the chain of command. If Perisic was as concerned as his letter to Milosevic indicates he was, he could have replaced Pavkovic immediately. He was his commander. He had absolute power to replace him, to remove him, but he didn't do that. On the contrary, on 10 January 1999, General Samardzic, commander of the 3rd Army, rated General Pavkovic as exceptional. That's in 4D136. And Vasiljevic told you that that was the highest possible rating at 8810 of the transcript. It's simply not possible that Samardzic would have rated General Pavkovic excellent if he was operating outside the chain of command, as General Perisic was contending. It's contended that, again by General Perisic, that Pavkovic would meet with Milosevic outside the chain of command, privately, secretly. The evidence presented on that was Vasiljevic said he saw him emerge from the White Palace at one point and concluded that he must have been meeting with Milosevic. And then later on in his testimony, Vasiljevic said, well, Milosevic had confirmed that he had met with Pavkovic, but that it was a private matter. Again, this has the characteristics of a red herring because it makes no difference if Pavkovic was meeting with Milosevic unless the Prosecution can show you that something came from those meetings that's relevant to the crimes charged in this indictment, and no showing has been made of that at all. There's no showing that General Pavkovic did something that's criminal as a result of a meeting that he had secretly with Milosevic. Why is this issue of outside the chain of command even before us in this case? The Prosecution contends that the VJ was being used illegally in Kosovo in 1998. And even though this evidence doesn't go to directly prove any allegation in the indictment, it's the position of the OTP that its evidence from which one might conclude, I guess, that if Pavkovic was operating illegally and outside the chain of command in 1998, he might also have been doing so in 1999. If that's the OTP position, this is not evidence capable of supporting a conviction, as required by the rule. 1998 actions do not provide direct proof of the commission of crimes during the indictment period. The key documents dealing with this issue have been mentioned by Mr. Sepenuk in his presentation: 4D137, the Perisic directive on use of the VJ of 28 July 1998. I'll not go into it further since Mr. Sepenuk did so. 4D140, July 29, General Ojdanic follows up that directive from Perisic and issues an order -- General Samardzic, I'm sorry, issues an order implementing the Perisic directive of the previous day, ordering the use of the VJ in exactly the way that he told Milosevic in his letter was not appropriate and illegal. The other document that was not mentioned by Mr. Sepenuk is 4D138, the Rules of Service of the Yugoslav Army that were in force in July of 1998. Paragraph 473 of that document makes it clear that army units may be used to combat outlawed, sabotage, terrorist, and other armed enemy groups. No declaration of emergency, imminent threat of war, or state of war is a prerequisite to the operation of this rule. Contrary to the allegations and even testimony of some witnesses, there's nothing in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that requires the army operate only in the border belt. There's no evidence in this record that General Pavkovic ordered anything illegal to be carried out, or that he learned of crimes and took no action upon them. One key document that is important in understanding the attitude of General Pavkovic and what he did is P1011. At page 80 of that document, you find an order by Pavkovic as the 3rd Army commander, a very urgent order by its terms, to treat humanely and spare the lives of members of enemy armed forces who surrender and lay down their arms or who are defeated, ordering compliance with the Geneva Convention. On the 17th of April, 14 days later, P1011, page 90, Pavkovic issues a warning that during the conduct of combat operations all provisions of international law of war and the instruction for the VJ members on the procedure in preparing and executing their tasks in Kosovo shall be fully implemented. Commands and professional organs shall undertake effective measures to prevent any forms of criminal acts as regulated, and then cites an order from the General Staff in that regard. When we talk about military prosecutors and military courts and what was done to investigate and punish, one thing that must be kept firmly in mind is the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in that regard. The document is P856, it's Article 136, which provides that the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia appoints military court judges and military prosecutors. They're appointed outside the chain of command of the Yugoslav Army. A commanding general of the Yugoslav Army has maybe nothing more than an advisory role in the appointment of these judges and prosecutors, and there's a reason for that. Judges and prosecutors in the military must operate independently, just like judges and prosecutors in the civilian system must operate independently. There wouldn't be any justice if commanders could order prosecutions or order prosecutions stopped or things of that nature. So what -- and Mr. Sepenuk even gave you some law in this regard. What's required of a commander if he learns of the commission of a crime is to report it to the military justice authorities, and after that he's done his job and it's up to them to go forward with it. The Prosecution witness Pesic testified that the Pristina Corps had its own separate military court and Prosecutor. The military district prosecutors were not subordinated to this Pristina Corps units. The Pristina Corps court and prosecutor, he said, were in operation from day one and processed a number of cases both during and after the bombing. You'll find this at 7275 through 7277. Touched upon by Mr. Sepenuk was Vasiljevic's investigation into crimes in Kosovo. You'll see that at page 8749. He describes how his investigations in Kosovo revealed that all crimes were being reported and processed. The only deficiency was in not reporting on up the chain of command. He said the feeling on the part of his security officers was that these crimes had been properly processed and that no further reporting was necessary. However, even in that milieu, you have to -- you have to understand what Vasiljevic is saying. He's saying that his security officers in Kosovo didn't report up through the security chain of command. He's not talking about the Pristina Corps not reporting up through the chain of command or the 3rd Army not reporting up through the chain of command. And again, Mr. Sepenuk has given you many examples of reports coming from the Pristina Corps to the 3rd Army, which also were copied to the General Staff. He referred to 5D84, which I refer you to just as an example. And then he also referred to a number of 3rd Army reports that went up to the General Staff talking about activities of the military prosecutor's office and what they were doing. At page 8750, Vasiljevic says this: "But I must say that those cases were not covered up or concealed. That was my impression. They didn't report it the way I suggested because the cases had already been prosecuted and processed. They simply thought that the problem had been resolved, the perpetrators had been arrested, and that's why they committed this omission in reporting." What did General Pavkovic do that will help you understand that the case against him is nonexistent? One thing you learned, both from testimony in the case and from your review of the -- the Coo material, was that General Pavkovic prior to his indictment was involved in assisting the Prosecution by turning over a large number of documents from the VJ to the Prosecution for their investigation. That's not something that is done by one with a guilty mind who believes that those documents will point to him in any way. You'll recall General Ojdanic summoning him to a meeting in Belgrade that was held on the 16th of May regarding reports of crimes being committed in Kosovo. And at that meeting, General Pavkovic said, I've looked into it. There's a dispute about who committed those crimes, and we really need to get to the bottom of it. I recommend we have a commission appointed to look into it immediately. Ojdanic agreed with that, that that needed to be done. That's not something you recommend, that's not something you try to get done if you believe the investigation by that commission is going to point at you. The next day they went to meet with Milosevic; Pavkovic and Ojdanic there, Sainovic was there. They recommended to Milosevic that what was needed was a commission, a joint commission, to go and investigate this commission of crimes in Kosovo. Ojdanic agreed, Sainovic agreed; unfortunately, Milosevic ignored the recommendation and did not approve of that. Nobody knows why. Nobody knows why he didn't think that was a good idea. But as a result of his rejection, it didn't happen. These things go directly to the intent and knowledge of Pavkovic, paragraph 54 of the indictment. It's not likely he would make this recommendation if he thought it would point to him, and the thing you must understand about these two meetings on the 16th and 17th of May is these were secret meetings. These were not open meetings. These were not meetings where there was press there. These were not meetings where the minutes were going to be distributed to the world. These were secret. Nobody was ever supposed to know about these meetings. And so when Pavkovic in these meetings recommends a commission, he's being genuine, he's being honest, and he's being serious. We can see that attitude as early as November 1998 in another secret meeting. This was a meeting of the interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism that met on the 2nd of November; it's Exhibit P2166. Pavkovic made a report at that meeting regarding the efforts that had been made in 1998 to suppress -- the successful efforts to suppress terrorism in Kosovo. On page 3, he said this -- and he was referring to a plan that had been put together to suppress terrorism in Kosovo during the summer offensive in 1998. Page 3, he said this: "As may be concluded, our plan was not to kill all the Siptars or expel them from Kosovo, but to destroy the main terrorist forces and separate the terrorists from the people." And, Judge Chowhan, that may be a partial answer to your question to Mr. Sepenuk, showing Mr. Pavkovic's concern for the Albanian people, that they separate the terrorists from them to protect them from those terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this pronouncement by Pavkovic, a plan not to kill or expel, occurs one month after the Prosecution alleges that this joint criminal enterprise came into existence; paragraph 20 of the indictment. Looking at the crime base in this case, it seems clear that most of the crimes were in late March and the month of April. By May, Pavkovic hears something about them, meets with Ojdanic, then Milosevic, recommends the commission. He believes they were mostly committed by non-VJ personnel, over whom he had no power to recommend prosecution. Thus, he wanted an independent commission to make sure that they would all be properly investigated and prosecuted. Milosevic's rejection of the Pavkovic recommend, I suggest, is highly exculpatory of Pavkovic, Ojdanic, and Sainovic. Those who had no fear welcomed an investigation; the one who did rejected it. It's difficult to imagine what more Pavkovic could have done. He drafted orders making it clear that he would not tolerate the commission of crimes. He made serious and successful efforts to get persons found to have committed crimes referred for prosecution. He tried to get this independent commission to investigate and was blocked in that regard. I want to now talk for just a few moments about the Prosecution's allegations regarding a Joint Command. The allegation of the existence of a Joint Command is a key part of the Prosecution's case for JCE and for Pavkovic's responsibility for crimes committed by all Serb forces, and I suggest to you this allegation fails. You can look through the evidence as long as you want to. You won't find any reports from any units to any Joint Command in the record of this case. The reports, the after-action reports, combat reports, remained in their normal chain of command throughout the indictment period in 1999. Reports addressed to a Joint Command would be a strong indication of the existence of that command, but there are none. There are, I believe, 13 Joint Command orders and decisions from the year 1999. They are P1966, P2031, P2015, P1968, P1969, P2003, P1970, P1973, P1974, P1975, P1976, P1878, and P1977. There are a number of curious things about these documents. Five of them range from the 22nd to the 28th of March; seven days. The other eight are the 14th, 15th, 16th, 2nd, and 9th of April; five days. So they all cover a period of only ten days -- or there are only ten days upon which they are issued. If you look at normal orders, action orders, orders to -- from the Pristina Corps, for instance, to engage in an action, at the end of that order -- at the end of almost any order that you'll see in this case, you'll see a distribution list where this order was distributed. If you look at the supposed Joint Command orders, there isn't any distribution list; it doesn't exist. There's no indication they were distributed to anyone. As I said, there are no after-action reports submitted to the Joint Command, even though these supposed Joint Command orders said that they should be. Where they're submitted is in the normal chain of command from the units to the Pristina Corps. There's no signatures on any of these documents; none of them are signed. And with no exception, if you look for the action order contained in these documents, you will see the language: "I have decided ..." That's really significant. "I have decided" means that that order is being drafted and decided by an individual, not by some Joint Command. Again, if you look at them, you will see that the only activity ordered in those orders is activity by units of the Pristina Corps; no activity by any MUP forces. These documents are simply not evidence of any Joint Command in operation during the indictment period in this case. What was going on, what these documents clearly show, because after the language "I have decided ...," you generally see the language: "... to support MUP forces." And what this is, is Pristina Corps orders where it was necessary for them to support MUP forces. So they were, at best, a coordination document, but certainly no evidence of any operating Joint Command that was giving orders to both VJ and MUP units. And you heard about that from Witness K25, who served in the PJP in Kosovo in 1998/1999. He said at page 2365 -- it's actually P2365 at page 21, that's his statement: "There was never any occasion in my experience where the VJ gave orders to the MUP, and although I'm aware that during a state of war under our laws the MUP could be subordinated to the VJ, this did not happen as far as I'm concerned." He goes on to say that from his experience, it was the MUP that was conducting combat operations against the KLA, while the VJ concerned itself primarily with deploying against the possibility of a NATO ground invasion. The VJ did provide heavy weapons support on occasion. I think some of the most crucial testimony you've heard in this case, and most credible in many ways, was the testimony of Shaun Byrnes, who came near the end. The thing that's remarkable about Shaun Byrnes in terms of the credibility of his testimony is that he's retired, he doesn't work for any government anymore. He's free to say what he wants to say, to tell you the truth about what he observed and what he saw and what he concluded from his time in Kosovo. At page 12198, he was asked by me: "I think with regard to your knowledge of General Pavkovic, what you've said about him was that he was direct and professional, and at one point you referred to him as a soldier's soldier who did not get involved in lectures on Serb history or politics. Is that a fair statement? "A. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, that's a fair statement. But let me point out for the record, I met General Pavkovic only once but I stand by what I said." With regard to the VJ: "Q. And with regard to the VJ, as you pretty much told us here today, your view of the VJ was that it conducted itself both professionally and honourably, both before and during the conflict, and in fact what you said about the shelling that was done with the heavy weaponry of the VJ was that it was not intended to cause casualties but more in the nature of causing harassment or fear. Is that fair? "A. That's what I said for the record earlier, yes." Now, that ties right in from what we heard from some of the villagers, that the shells were going over the tops of their villages and not landing in them, like they were shelling something across on the other side of the village. That's these kinds of new warfare I was talking about earlier, where there's a great need to try to separate the civilian population from the combatants, and that's one way you might do that. Back to the Joint Command issue, in July 1998 while Pavkovic was commander of the Pristina Corps and Samardzic was the 3rd Army commander, we got another clue about how the army viewed this supposed Joint Command. You'll recall that in Exhibit 4D91, Samardzic authorises Pavkovic to attend Joint Command meetings; however, before attending, he was required to brief the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army about proposals that would be made at that meeting for the engagement of forces. And then only with the consent of the Chief of Staff could he attend the meeting and approve. After the meeting, he was then required to again report to the Chief of Staff on any proposals that were accepted and any subsequent requests which might diverge from previous proposals, and seek consent from General Samardzic or the Chief of Staff for those requests. He was required to inform the Joint Command of the 3rd Army about decisions regarding the requests. Clearly, even in 1998, the Joint Command could only propose joint participation by the army, and the 3rd Army command would have to approve; it could not be ordered by the Joint Command. The OTP alleges that General Pavkovic was involved in some kind of cover-up. In its pre-trial brief with regard to JCE, the Prosecution suggested that the accused took steps to prevent investigations and engaged in a considerable operation to conceal the commission of crimes in Kosovo. These efforts are said by the OTP to be a reflection of guilty knowledge. Remember what Vasiljevic said after investigating in Kosovo: "I must say that those cases were not covered up or concealed." There's simply no evidence before you at all that General Pavkovic took any steps whatsoever to conceal any crimes in Kosovo; the evidence is contrary, calling for a commission to try to bring light to them. Count 1 and Count 2 deal with deportation and forcible transfer. It's clear that people were leaving Kosovo in large numbers; it's not clear why they were doing so. There's evidence that they left because of fear of NATO bombing; there's evidence they left because the KLA told them to leave; there's evidence they left because of fighting between KLA and Serb forces in their area; there's evidence they left because they were told to do so by Serb forces; there's evidence they left because they were told to do so by Serb civilians. What there is not is evidence capable of supporting a conviction of Pavkovic for deportation as charged in this count of the indictment. There's no order from Pavkovic ordering deportation of people. K25, again the PJP soldier: "Whenever we have an operation in a village, there are always going to be civilians who are taken out of the combat activity zone. We call that taking the refugees and placing them behind the line of blockade." That's in P2365, page 9. With regard to the KLA, evidence from witnesses that the KLA told people to leave their villages, evidence that the KLA were trying to get sympathy from the international community, see P680, the OSCE fusion working papers. That's P689. Halimi left Zabar because a KLA member told him he should leave for his own safety. That's transcript P4447. The KLA used people as human shields. That was Zyrapi, 2448. Judge Bonomy asked Zyrapi at page 5949 of the transcript that -- said to him: "Your answer suggests that you increased the risk by keeping the population in the area where the KLA are in control." Counts 3 and 4 are murder counts. For 98 bis purposes, murders have been proven; however, there's no evidence capable of supporting a conviction that shows that any murders were committed by forces under the command and control of General Pavkovic or with his encouragement or support or on his order. Persecutions, Count 5, there's no evidence capable of supporting a conviction that any crime charged in this count was committed by forces or persons under the command or control of General Pavkovic or with his encouragement or support. As to the responsibility of General Pavkovic under 7(1), Mr. O'Sullivan has accurately stated the law in his presentation. He's charged with ordering, and there's no evidence that he ordered the commission of any crimes. He's charged with planning, and there's no evidence that he planned the commission of any crimes. He's charged with instigating, and there's no evidence that he instigated the commission of any crimes. And there's no evidence that he aided or abetted in any crimes. As to 7(3), there's no evidence that General Pavkovic from his position of authority as 3rd Army commander failed in any way to prevent or punish the commission of crimes by persons under his control. The evidence is that he did all that could be expected or is required of a person in his position. All international witnesses who met him gave you a very positive assessment of him: a good soldier, a competent soldier, direct, a soldier's soldier. All the Prosecution can give you in terms of evidence against General Pavkovic is what I call a might-have/must-have/could-have argument, and that doesn't work, even at this stage of the case. This evidence fails and is not capable of supporting a conviction, and you should acquit General Pavkovic on all the counts against him. Thank you so much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, are you anxious to start this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just wondering whether it might be superfluous for me to spoil both your evening and tomorrow. Perhaps it might be best if I were to spoil only tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've already succeeded in spoiling my evening by not -- by not reaching 7.00. So you can complete the picture tomorrow, which will be at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will make up for the loss of time tomorrow, I promise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll rise now, and we'll sit at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
